In
the remarks I shall make this evening with reference to the Nanaimo trouble I will endeavour to avoid any repetition of any remarks I may have made on February 6, when the debate commenced; but it may be necessary to refer to what was stated to be the initial cause, that is, the discrimination against Messrs. Mottishaw and Portrey, the two members of the gas committee. This cause was evidently lost sight of in the later stages of the trouble which resolved itself into the straight question, the recognition of the United Mine Workers of America. I shall say a few words as to the manner in which this strike was caused. I have had a mining experience of over forty years and have been in several strikes and mining troubles, but never in the whole of my experience did I know of a strike which was inaugurated in the manner in which the strike on Vancouver island was inaugurated. There is a well established principle amongst miners that those who wish to go on strike for any grievance or for bettering their condition shall only do so by and with the consent of a good majority of the whole. If I recollect correctly it requires a two-thirds majority of those entitled to vote upon the question as to whether or not there shall be a strike. The vote to return to work requires, I think, only a majority. This strike was not inaugurated upon those principles, and I venture to say that if this strike fails-and I think it will fail, in fact it probably has failed-its failure will be in a great measure due to the fact that the strike was not inaugurated
upon the principles which I have enunciated. With reference to the initial cause of the strike, the discrimination against Messrs. Mottishaw and Portrey, this matter came up in the British Columbia Legislature in the reply of the Premier to Mr. Place, the Socialist member for Newcastle. The Premier proceeded to quote from a report by Mr. Mottishaw to the effect that No. 2 mine at Extension was not in a dangerous condition at the time the agitation about the gas committee originated. He regarded it as rather a peculiar thing that the report which was supposed to be fundamental in the support of the trouble did not state that the mine was in unsafe condition. Referring to Mr. Place, the Premier said:
My friend from Newcastle has not been behind hand in this matter and I have read his speeches on the subject. He tries his best by all the ingenuity he can command to show that this Government and this Government alone, is at the bottom of the whole trouble, when he knows perfectly well, because he can be fair-minded if he wants to, that what was behind the difficulty was the proposal to establish the United Mine Workers of America on the island.
During this trouble the companies, at least in my constituency, were at all times ready to meet their men as a body of miners, but they absolutely refused to meet them as a committee emanating from the United Mine Workers of America. The question will naturally be asked, why did the operators refuse to meet the United Mine Workers of America? I do not propose to go into that matter, because it was threshed out very thoroughly on the 6th and 10th of February and also this afternoon.
But the main feature was that of recognition. Probably many hon. members of the House do not understand what is meant by recognition. If you will pardon me, Mr. Speaker, I will quote from the Coal Age of New York. I want to be perfectly frank in this matter and to state that this publication has been decidedly opposed to the methods used by the United Mine Workers of America on Vancouver island. It says in its issue of February 21, 1914:
' It seems only right and proper at this time to ask what is implied in the demand for recognition, so urgently and persistently made by labour unions in general, but with marked pertinacity and daring by the United Mine Workers of America in particular. There is a legitimate use of this term which may be understood to convey so much no one will deny. Recognition is to be earned, not demanded. It is the ripened fruit of toil, labour and industry. It comes naturally as the result of accomplishment. There must be something to recognize in order to gain recognition.

There can be no objection, as a rule, to operators recognizing a mine union. Many of the mines to-day are working under that principle. There is a distinct understanding between the operators and the men. The unions are fully recognized, and as a *rule the result is that the conditions prevailing are absolutely harmonious. But 'there is something underlying this; it is not simply recognizing the United Mine Workers of America that the operators <object to. There is evidently something underlying, some ulterior object, as has been stated by the hon. Minister of Labour and by my hon. friend from Perth, and 'that is that the United Mine Workers are using the labour unions to virtually control the coal trade conditions on the Pacific coast. I will not dwell upon that matter; I mention that for what it is worth, but that is one of the things which it is hard to prove, and the only proof we have is Mr. Farrington's own statement.
Why did the miners of Vancouver island join the United Mine Workers of America? It has been stated by the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) that this was the initial union upon the island, that up to that time the men were absolutely disorganized. I beg to correct him. There have been miners' unions on Vancouver island for thirty or forty years, and some of the most severe struggles we have had have been under the direction of labour unions. It is true that there was no organized labour union at the time that the United Mine Workers of America invaded the island, but there have been miners' unions, and some of them have been very successful indeed. I might mention one in my own town of Nanaimo, where the conditions were so amicable that the mine manager became the president of it. You can readily understand that when a mine owner or mine operator consents to be the president of a labor union things must be [DOT]amicable.
The hon. member for South Cape Breton said that Orientals should not be employed as miners, shot lighters or in positions of confidence or trust. He made the statement that within a very short period the number of Orientals employed in connection with the mines of British Columbia had risen from ten per cent not underground, to 65 per cent above and below ground. If I am wrong in that I hope the hon. gentleman will correct me. I fail to see how the hon. member can support that statement when I show the House that the conditions prohibiting the employment of.

Orientals in large numbers is absolutely safeguarded by the Coal Mines Regulations Act of British Columbia. I quote section 56:
(1)	Coal-miners' certificates of competency shall be granted by a board of examiners consisting of not less than three competent persons ; such board to be constituted at each colliery which the Lieutenant Governor in Council may designate, and such board shall consist of the following persons:
(a)	One appointed by the Lieutenant Governor in Council:
(b)	One, with two alternates, appointed by the manager or managers of the colliery:
(c)	One coal-miner with two alternates, possessed of certificates of competency as such. Such coal-miner and coal-miner alternates shall be elected by the coal-miners whose names shall appear on the list referred to in section 12 in the Third Schedule to this Act:
(d)	The proceedings of the board shall be in accordance with the rules in the Third Schedule to this Act.
I want hon. members to pay particular attention to this, because this clause was inserted at my suggestion and with the hearty approval of the Minister of Mines:
(e)	An inspector of mines snail, ex-officio, be a member, without voting power, of all boards under this section within his inspectorate.
(2)	Such board shall hold office for one year or until their successors are appointed.
(3)	The examination as aforesaid shall be held on the first Monday in each and every month, except in cases where the minister may fix some other date on whicn a board shall hold its examinations.
The reason why he was divested of voting powers was that it would disturb the balance of the board and .make it .an even number, and consequently in many cases inoperative.
No certificate of competency shall be granted to any coal-miner who does not satisfy the majority of such Board of Examiners that he is sufficiently conversant with the English language, and with the provisions of the Acts relating to coal-mining and the rules and regulations made thereunder, to render his employment as such safe, and also that he has been employed in a coal mine for at least twelve months previous to the date of his application for such certificate, and has sufficient knowledge of methods of coal-mining to render him competent to perform the duties appertaining to his employment.
Therefore, I fail to see how, under these restrictions, it would be possible that a wholesale increase in the .employment of Orientals in the mines of British Columbia could take place. The inspector was placed on that Board for the reason that he should exercise no authority as to voting power but supervision over all applicants applying to that board for a certificate, and to see that, in

addition to being competent miners, they should possess an absolute knowledge of the English language, or such as to enable them to read, not only the Coal Mines Regulations Act, but any notices of danger or other publications which might be posted about the mines for the general safety of the mines. Under these conditions it would be impossible to import Orientals in a wholesale manner, as the hon. member for South Cape Breton would have this House believe. That there w.as an increase I believe, but that the increase was not over and above the number that the machinery of the board could allow to pass through is I think beyond question. The board sits once a month, and the time is fully occupied in getting ten or fifteen through at a sitting. That being the case, I fail to see how a large increase in the number of Orientals, over and above those already there, could possibly take place. They were certainly not imported. The Orientals, as I said on the 6th ultimo, are only employed underground in the mines of the Canadian Collieries Company. They are employed, as a matter of course, on the surface at other collieries.

I have been given to understand that the Act of British Columbia has been amended since the Act that my hon. friend read, in some particulars that affect the employment of Orientals. Is that a fact or is it not?

The Act has not been amended. 1 am in a position to know, because I am responsible for the drafting of that Act, and I know it is not the intention, unless a very urgent case demanded it, to re-open the Act.

The information I had
was possibly inaccurate. Does the hon. gentleman say there have been no amendments to the regulations based on the Act?

There have been no
amendments whatever to the Act; the Act has not been re-opened for any purpose. It may naturally be asked why Orientals are only employed in the mines of the Canadian collieries:-

What would happen
if a man should go to work in a mine without having complied with the regulation which the hon. gentleman has read?

Do you mean if he
went to the mine without a certificate?
Yes.

If he goes before the committee and is refused a certificate, he cannot be employed, and if the manager does employ him he is guilty of an infringement of the Act, the penalties for which are provided in a general section.
That is what I wanted to know.

It is a matter of
pretty ancient history why the Canadian Collieries, Limited, originally the Duns-muir Mines, should be allowed to employ Chinese underground, and why they are not employed underground in any other mine in British Columbia. They used to be employed in all the mines on the island, and in the year 1887 a disastrous explosion occurred in the No. 1 mine of the Western Fuel Company, then the New Vancouver Coal Company. Chinese and white men were employed underground in the mine, and there were approximately 100 lives lost, a great number being Chinamen. The sentiment prevailed that possibly the explosion and consequent deplorable loss of life may have been due to the inexperience of the Chinamen. That sentiment became so strong that the miners refused to resume work after the mine was restored, and the company willingly acquiesced that from that time forward no Orientals should be employed for any purpose whatever underground. This decision was followed by all the mines on Vancouver island, with the exception of the Dunsmuirs. The Orientals have been employed in the Dunsmuir mine for over a quarter of a century, probably thirty years.
It may be asked, why has some legislation not been passed prohibiting Orientals from being employed underground. As a matter of fact, such legislation has been passed, and its legality was submitted to the Privy Council in the friendly case of Bryden vs. the Wellington Collieries Company. The point in the case was as to the validity or otherwise of the clause prohibiting the employment of Chinese underground in any capacity whatever. "The decision of the Privy Council was that the clause of the Act was ultra vires, and consequently, under that ruling of the Privy Council, the Canadian Collieries and Dunsmuirs have enjoyed the advantage, if I may so term it, of employing Chinese from that day to this. This in an unfair condition; it gives them distinct advantage, not only with regard to trade, but it is eminently unfair and unjust to the white



workers. I trust I have made myself perfectly clear as to how I stand upon the question of the employment of Orientals underground.

I understood the hon.
gentleman to read from a .statute of British Columbia a provision which prevents the employment of a miner underground, except he passes a certain examination. I understand the hon. gentleman now to say that, according to ancient practice, Orientals are now employed in these Dunsmuir collieries.
Exactly.
How is it that the Act is not effective against them, if it is effective against other mines in the province?

The provision of the
Act that no Orientals should be employed underground was declared ultra vires by the Privy Council. This is not embodied in the present Act, and the only restriction against the Orientals in the present Act is that they shall be able to speak and Tead the English language, and shall be practical miners. There are, however, other restrictions, which my hon. friend from South Cape Breton referred to, and which I shall read. Rule 42 provides:
No Chinaman or person unable to speak English shall be appointed to or shall occupy any position of trust or responsibility in or about a mine whereby through his ignorance, carelessness, or negligence, he may endanger the life or limb of any person employed in or about a mine, namely:	as banksmen, onsetter, signalman,
brakeman, switchman, furnaceman, engineer, or be employed at the windlass of a sinking pit.
These are the positions which he is not allowed to occupy underground, but there is evidently no provision preventing him from acting as a miner, providing he can produce before the Board of Examiners tne qualification required.
There is another question; and I wish to avoid, as far as possible, any partisan controversy while I am speaking upon this question. One hon. member on the other side of the House compared the visit of the ex-Minister of Labour, Mr. Mackenzie King, with that of the present Minister of Labour, with regard to the settlement of strikes on Vancouver island, and he quoted the instance of the strike at Nanaimo in 1905, when the ex-Minister of Labour went out and amicably adjusted that strike very satisfactqrily. This was used in compari-. son with the action of the present Minister of Labour, in the light that he had failed
[Mr. Shepherd.!
where the former Minister of Labour had been so eminently successful. I wish to point out that the conditions were entirely different. The strike in 1905 was called upon the very principle I enunciated at the commencement of my remarks. There was a distinct grievance; there was a unanimous vote that they should strike until the grievance was redressed. I cannot Temember the'duration of that strike; I think it was about six weeks; but about that time the opportunity had arrived for a compromise or for some one to intervene, and the Hon. Mackenzie King came out and did effect a reconciliation and a readjustment of the grievances which then existed.
But, what were the conditions when the present Minister of Labour came to Nanaimo? When I returned home, after last session of Parliament, I thoroughly investigated in my own way the conditions prevailing, and I came to the conclusion then, and I have had no occasion since I formed that opinion to change it, that the difficulty was absolutely insoluble, so far as compromise was concerned. The operators absolutely refused to acknowledge the United Mine Workers of America, and the United Mine Workers of America absolutely refused to deal with the operators unless they were received as the United Mine Workers of America. When you get conditions such as these, a solution is absolutely impossible. These conditions confronted the Minister of Labour when he visited Nanaimo with Mr. Price. These were the conditions when Nanaimo was visited by the deputy minister of labour. There was no other conclusion to arrive at than that a solution was absolutely impossible so far as any intervention was concerned. I recall the remark made by the minister to a body of miners in Nanaimo who had called to interview him with regard to some solution of the matter. He said: ' The question is this, gentlemen: one of the parties must back down, and back down all the way.' That has been the inevitable result.
This being the condition, I think that the comparison was absolutely unfair. Would the ex-Minister of Labour have been as successful with the strike of 1913-14 as he was in 1905? I submit not.. Would the exminister have gone so far in his efforts to effect a reconciliation and have advised the operators to accept recognition of the United Mine Workers of America? I venture to say not. He would have accomplished no more in his efforts at reconciliation than was

accomplished by my hon. friend the Minister of Labour.
One more word about recognition. Why was the association so particularly anxious that it should be recognized? The reason is that recognition carries with it the right to deduct from every worker a certain portion of his earnings for the purposes of the union. If the miners are united, why should it be necessary for the union to compel the companies to deduct this fee from the regular earnings of their miners? For the simple reason that the men are untrue to each other. There is a lack of solidarity among the workers, and therein they fail. So long as this lack of solidarity continues among the workers, so long will they continue to fail. The fault and failure lies with that entirely.
I do not wish to dwell any further upon this phase of the trouble; but there is another phase of this question. The strike, so far as the operators are concerned, is virtually over. The mines are working to their utmost capacity, that is, as far as the mines in their present condition will allow; because it must be admitted that the damage done to the mines is considerable. In the strike zone there must be about a thousand men unemployed, who are still loyal to the United Mine Workers of America, and who are receiving strike pay. A number of their coworkers are undergoing sentences in jail, and it is upon this matter that I wish to speak for a little while. In my opinion if there is one thing above another which will tend to bring industrial peace and quiet to the troubled strike zone of Vancouver island, it will be the extension of clemency to these imprisoned miners. I know many of these miners, and I know that they are not criminals at heart. They have been ill-advised; they have been led away in the heat of the moment; and I think that the demands of society are reasonably satisfied by the sentences that some of them have already served. I am pleased to note that the learned judge who is conducting these cases is of the same opinion. In confirmation of this, I must ask you to bear with me while I read hii remarks to a body of men whom he released on suspended sentence. Mr. Justice Morrison addressed the men as follows:
In regard to the commissions of some crimes I quite agree with the proposal urged by some of the leading criminologists, that when an accused person has been tried and found guilty of a crime the court instead of punishing the crime should proceed to inquire who is the offender and what are his character and 82i
antecedents and circumstances; and upon the result of that inquiry he should be dealt with in whatever way the interests of the public-demand. The effect would be that some offenders who now go to prison would be restored to the ranks of labour. That must not be mistaken for leniency.
We are more in need of prison reform fWfetv leniency. At the same time I do not believe that severity in punishment will avail to check crime. Great severity in punishment of crime is now as obsolete as many of the barbaric methods of the old days.
Now, I think you are not of the criminal class. You have been up to the time of this particular offense, lawabiding citizens who in my opinion have been betrayed into the present trouble by designing agencies whose machinations it was most difficult to resist. You can assist in making those reforms. If my treatment of you to-day will tend in any way to bring the administration of the law into contempt on account of its apparent leniency then indeed will any attempt, at reform be in vain.
1 hope you will not think I am taking advantage of Your present position to foist upon you gratuitous advice. I wish you to know that it is a mistake to assume that because you may think you have a grievance that therefore you may commit a breach of the law with impunity. We all think we have grievances. But we must not in any attempt to remedy those grievances take the law into our bands.
I do not mean anything I have said to cast any reflection upon properly organized labour I am sure that had you taken the advice of some of yjur representatives in the legislature, and honourable members of your un.ons there would have been no breaches of the peace. It would be affectation for me to pretend that I do not hear of the pernicious influence at work upon the men-influences which were brought into requisition in and about those very assizes and of which unfortunately you have been vicarious victims.
In spite of those agencies and their ill-advised futile resolutions I shall now, after mature consideration, do that which were it r.ot for such blatant conduct on their part would have been done considerably sooner.
I am in no way influenced by them or their advisers in extending to you that consideration which I think your cases respectively merit and which I think is entirely in the public interest.
Application was made to the Minister oi Justice for clemency in some cases, and it was not considered that the time was opportune to extend clemency. On account of the troubles at Nanaimo and on Vancouver Island an organization was formed for the purpose of endeavouring to secure the release of these men who were imprisoned. That this organization did more harm than good to their fellow-workmen, I am thoroughly convinced. The meetings were attended by men who spoke intemperately, and who used violent language, threatening language; and, instead of approaching the Minister of Justice in a contrite manner, they approached him absolutely demand-

ing the release of these men as if they were suffering an injustice. And it must be borne in mind that many of these men pleaded guilty, and the rest of them were tried by a jury of their peers.
Now, Sir, there is still another side of this question to be considered; and, removing it from its local colouring, I submit that there is a widespread dissatisfaction and unrest among the workers of the world. There must be some cause for it. When, owing to the high cost of living and other causes it becomes so difficult for workingmen to make both ends meet, can any one fail to understand that workers are prone to lawlessness and crime? And is it not the duty of all legislative bodies, and the duty of the State, to endeavour as far as possible to remove the causes that drive men to lawlessness and crime? I am reminded, Sir, [DOT]of the words of the author from whom I -quoted before, Charles Dickens, in Martin Chuzzlewit, from which I shall make a brief quotation in conclusion. The case today seems very similar to that of which Dickens speaks. I would recommend this quotation to the Minister of Justice when I again ask him to present to His Royal Highness the Governor General a further appeal for clemency on behalf of these imprisoned miners, believing, as I do, that it is the shortest cut to peace and industrial prosperity for my stricken town and district. In a state of society which ignores the causes which lead to lawlessness and crime, I cannot put my views more clearly than in the following words of Dickens:
No, my good Sir, I have a duty to discharge which I owe to society, and it shall he discharged, my friend, at any cost.'
O late remembered much forgotten mouthing braggart duty, always owed and seldom paid in any other coin but punishment and wrath, when will mankind begin to know thee? When will men acknowledge thee in thy neglected cradle and thy stunted youth, and not begin their recognition in thy sinful manhood and thy desolate old age? O ermined judge whose duty to society is now to doom the ragged -criminal to punishment and death, hadst thou never, man, a duty to discharge in barring up the hundred open gates that wooed him to the felon's dock and throwing but ajar the portals of a decent life?
O prelate, whose duty to society it is to mourn in melancholy, phrase the sad degeneracy of these bad times in which thy lot of honours has been cast, did nothing go before thy elevation to the lofty seat from which thou dealest out thy homilies to other tarriers for dead men's shoes, whose duty to society has not begun?
O magistrate, so rare a country gentleman and brave a squire, had you no duty to society before the ricks were blazing and the mob was mad? Or did it spring up armed and booted from the earth, a corps of yeomanry full grown?

I speak with all sincerity when I say that I have listened with great interest to the very moderate and very reasonable address of my hon. friend from Nanaimo (Mr. Shepherd). I think he has impressed every member within the sound of his voice as he has impressed me. I think we can quite realize that my hon. friend occupies a very unenviable position in regard to this important labour dispute in his own community, in his own constituency, in his own home, and I can understand the great difficulty he would have in attempting to discuss a question of this magnitude in its peculiar local and personal conditions. Of course, he has discussed the matter so far as it relates to mining, with a knowledge that few of us possess. In speaking on this subject, I confess that, from a practical standpoint, I have but little knowledge. But 1 have read the report on the subject published by the minister. I have also read the return brought down in answer to the motion of my hon. friend from Maison-neuve (Mr. Verville), and that in answer to the motion of the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). Besides, I have been receiving a large correspondence from the hon. gentleman's own city and other parts of British Columbia since this matter was discussed in the House three or four weeks ago.
If I am able hurriedly to summarize the substance of my hon. friend's address this evening, I come to the conclusion that it practically amounts to three things. He first lays down the position that this strike is on the question of whether or not the mining companies shall recognize the United Mine Workers of America. His second important conclusion is that a law exists in the province of British Columbia, of which he claims -to be the father, by which they can prevent Asiatics and certain classes of labourers from going down into the mines to perform work there, but from necessity-I fear from political necessity-this law has not been invoked by the powers that be in British Columbia. The third important conclusion at which he arrived is that, through the blundering of some person or bodies of persons, this unfortunate dispute has reached a point where he himself has come to the conclu-; sion that it is impossible of settlement.
Now, I have tried to summarize-and I think I have done it fairly-the main points of the argument of my hon. friend. As I have said, I realize the local conditions and difficulties of my hon. friend in

attempting to discuss it from the general standpoint of whether or not the Minister of Labour is liable to the censure of this House for the part he has played or has not played. For that is the question we are discussing here to-night; that is the substance of the motion of my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville). In effect, the hon. member for Maisonneuve says that the Minister of Labour has not properly enforced the law, that he has not done his duty by the miners of British Columbia, and that he deserves to be censured by this House. I quite understand the difficulty my hon. friend from Nanaimo has in trying to discuss this matter from that reasonable standpoint. I give him credit for not having referred to the Minister of Labour except once. When the Minister of Labour went to British Columbia in June, when the heather was afire, when men were at one another's throats, he came to the conclusion that the difficulty had reached the point where some one had not only to back down but to back clear down; and, as he concluded that his friends the magnates of British Columbia could not back clear down-and I think I could go further and say that the hon. member for Nanaimo knows his man too well to think that the Minister of Labour would ask his friends the magnates to back down -he agrees with the Minister of Labour in saying that at that time it was impossible to do anything because the magnates could not back down.
As I have said, I have been receiving many communications from British Columbia within the last three or four weeks. Some of them are really surprising, startling, to me. From these communications, and also from the correspondence brought down by the minister, I think any reasonable man, any man who approaches this subject with an open mind, must have the conclusion forced upon him that there is the possibility of an unholy alliance existing between Premier McBride, the Conservative party of British Columbia, the Canadian Northern railway, or the firm of Mackenzie and Mann, and the Minister of Labour. I do not say this alliance does exist, but I do say that is the conclusion to which one is irresistibly driven who reads this correspondence.
The minister will say: What proof have you of that? I am going to give him the proof, and I hope he will answer it. I have gone over this return fairly carefully, and have tried to summarize it, and I will
give my hon. ~ friend some of the arguments on which I base these assertions. Take first the conduct of the minister and his department, and when I say his department, of- course I mean the minister, because not only is he technicaly responsible, but I do not believe that any act or move was made by his department without the minister's personal knowledge, and therefore I treat the minister as being the department. I find that a day or two after the strike was inaugurated, the minister sent a telegram to a representative of the miners in British Columbia that he had noticed that there were difficulties, and he took the trouble to point out to them, which they probably knew as well as the minister, the procedure under the Industrial Disputes Act, and stated that he was sending them copies of an application form if they wished to avail themselves of the benefits of the Industrial Disputes Act. I am not go:ng into an argument as to whether these documents were sent or not. Five weeks after, the secretary of the miners union sent back a letter stating that they had never received the documents and one of the officials replied that the documents were forwarded. I do not wish to discuss it any longer. I only give the fact that one party says they sent the documents and the other party says they did not. A most remarkable corroboration of the ground taken by the men however is to be found in one of the letters of Mr. Farrington in which he states that, on the second occasion when the minister stated that he was sending copies of these documents to Mr. Farrington, they were not enclosed in the letter. So it is remarkable that on two occasions when the minister or his department professed to be sending a form to these miners on which to make the application to take advantage of the Industrial Disputes Act, the documents never reached the miners. Then I find that' about the same time the minister sent a telegram to the mine workers-and here the minister had no doubt whatever as to whom he should send the correspondence because he sends it straight to Mr. D. B. Hanna, one of the vice presidents of the Canadian Northern railway, of course, closely connected with Mackenzie and Mann, and I have no douot at all the proper party to whom to send any information regarding the coal strike in British Columbia. Mr. Hanna replies as follows, (page 11 of the return to the motion of my hen. friend from Maisonneuve) :

Toronto, Ont, Sept. 24, 1912.
F. A. Acland, Esq.,
Deputy Minister of Labour,
Ottawa, Ont.
Your message 21st only received yesterday, but not being on board I waited to consult Sir William and have since wired Victoria for information. We thank minister for his offer and will state situation more fully when I receive reply from Victoria. Meanwhile understand men at one mine have quit work but trouble not spreading.
(Sgd.) D. B. Hanna.
That was on the 24th of September in reply to a telegram sent to Mr. Hanna three days earlier. On the 27th day of September. 19X2, a further correspondence took place between Mr. Acland, the deputy minister and the coal mining company.
Ottawa, Sept. 27, 1912.
Re disturbances in coal mines at Ladysmith and Cumberland, B.C.
Dear Sir,-With further reference to the industrial troubles in the coal mines controlled by your company on Vancouver island concerning which the department has exchanged telegrams with you, the minister, I am to state, is particularly desirous of having without delay your company's statement on the subject, and would be obliged if the same could be forwarded immediately. Statements received by the minister go to show that work has ceased at Ladysmith as well as Cumberland, the alleged ground being discrimination against membership in the local union, but the department is not fully informed as to this. The situation is one in which it would appear probable that an application would shortly be received for a board of conciliation and investigation, and the minister has thought that your company might desire to take action which will render unnecessary the establishment of such a board. Can you kindly arrange to have a statement expressing the company's view forwarded to the department so that it may he placed before the minister on Monday, the 30th?
Tours very truly,
9 p-m.	(Sgd) F. A. Acland,
Deputy Minister of Labour.
D. B. Hanna, Esq.,
Third Vice-Pres., Canadian Northern Ry., Toronto, Ont.
As I said, the minister asked the railway company to send to him their statement of the case and, as I shall show later on, he also asked the men to send to him their statement of the case. One would think that to a communication of that importance, coming from the Department of Labour over as important a matter as this coal strike, the Canadian Northern railway would have at least, as a matter of courtesy, favoured the minister with a reply; but the conduct of the Canadian Northern, or perhaps I should call them the Canadian Collieries, was such

that it might be said that they treated the minister with what would almost appear like mild contempt. I want to read the correspondence to show you how hard the minister tried to get the information and how fearfully afraid the Canadian Collieries were of the Minister of Labour. I wish to show you, Sir, what a wonderful bond of union must have existed between these two great personages. There is considerable correspondence in a general way between Mr. Acland, the deputy minister, and the mining company. That was in September and the early part of October and then the whole matter dropped. Now you come down to the 19th day of November, that is a month and a half had elapsed and nothing was done, hundreds of men were out of employment and a terrific condition of affairs existed all through one of the great coal mining centres of Canada; and after about five or six weeks the correspondence opened up again and in the letter of the 19th of November, 1912, we find a statement which I think is of more than passing importance. It shows that they did not, for some reason, want to commit to paper what was going on between the minister and his friends. That is the substance of it. But they actually sent the deputy minister to Toronto to talk this matter over privately and verbally with the company and get the company's views without putting them on paper; and so well did the company guard the matter that they have never put their views on paper. I do not know what information the minister may have, but so far as the miners are concerned or the public or Parliament, down to this day we are in absolute ignorance of the position taken by the company. We perhaps know their position and that is that they will not treat with the men, they will not treat with anybody, but the reasons which they give are a closed book in so far as we are concerned.
I shall read first the letter of the 19th of November, 1912:
Dear Mr. Hanna:
When I called on you on me 9th instant regarding the coal mining troubles of your company's mines on Vancouver island you were good enough to promise to secure a statement of circumstances to date and asked your Mr. Thompson to see to it. I had intended calling on you on the following Saturday, the 16th inst., but did not reach Toronto until your offices were closed. Perhaps you will be kind enough to forward for the minister's information the statement you were expecting, if it has in the meantime arrived. Parliament, as you are aware, meets immediately and the minister feels it would be well to have the latest information

from the company's point of view as to this somewhat difficult dispute.
Yours truly,
(Sgd) F. A. Acland,
*	Deputy Minister of Labour.
D. B. Hanna, Esq.,
Third Vice-Pres., Canadian Northern Railway, Toronto, Ont.
This was answered on the 21st of November by Mr. Hanna, as follows:
Toronto, Ont., November 21, 1912.
F. A. Acland, Esq.,
Deputy Minister of Labour,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Mr. Acland,-I have your letter of the 19th instant. I understand from Mr. F. C. Annesley, secretary to our president, that he sent to Sir William at Ottawa on the 18th instant some papers concerning the difficulty at the mines on Vancouver island, and no doubt Sir William has since taken the matter up with you.
Will you please advise me if such is not the case.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd) D. B. Hanna.
That is followed by a communication from the department to Mr. Hanna, dated November 23, 1912:
Ottawa, November 23, 1912. Dear Mr. Hanna,-Yours of the 21st. Sir William, as you say, has been in Ottawa for some days, but has not, I think, been in the department and has not left with the minister or elsewhere any papers or information concerning the difficulties at your mines. If you are able to apprise the minister of the latest developments and present situation it would be an advantage. It frequently happens that questions on matters of this kind are asked in. Parliament and the minister particularly desires to have information at hand.
Yours truly,
F. A. Acland,
Deputy Minister of Labour. D. B. Hanna, Esq.,
Third Vice-President,
Canadian Northern Railway Company, Toronto, Ont.
The last document in this remarkable series, dated November 26,	1912, and
headed Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, Toronto, reads as follows:
F. A. Acland,
Deputy Minister of Labour,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Sir,-With regard to your letter to Mr. D. B. Hanna, respecting trouble at the local mines, Sir William Mackenzie is going to Ottawa to-night. Will you therefore kindly communicate with him while there. I may say that we understood that Colonel Davidson had seen either you or the minister with regard to this matter.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd) H. Annesley.
That is all the information which the Canadian Northern Railway Company gave the public regarding this most important
transaction. If they gave the minister anything else he has deliberately concealed it from Parliament. I make that statement advisedly after having read all the returns brought down by the minister and after having listened to practically every word said on this subject, not only in this debate, but in the previous debates in this House. But you have to go back to the telegram sent by Mr. Annesley to Sir William Mackenzie some time prior to that in order to see the true significance of the conduct of the company and the conduct of the minister. I find on page 17 of this report a most remarkable document, and I am afraid it must have been smuggled in without the minister's knowledge, because it is not directed to the department. It was handed in by the Canadian Northern railway people, and I think it ixplains the whole situation. The trouble began about the 17th of September, and this is dated only a few days afterwards. It is as follows:
Canadian Northern Railway Company,
Office of the Third Vice-President,
Toronto, 7 th Oct., 1912.
Coulson wires: Referring to my telegram of the 10th I did not state that two weeks ago our miners were prevented from voting on resumption work by local union president who destroyed ballot boxes and also threatened men. Local union officials realize error in not giving thirty days' notice before striking and also in not having consulted international union and are trying to avert responsibility. International union repudiate action and will not support strike morally or financially. Conditions very quiet, but we expect men very soon to hold indignation meeting and return to work repudiating union entirely. Union appeal to Ottawa their last resort. If unsuccessful union dead and labour trouble ended.
Message endorsed.
Telephone out of order.
(Signed) F. C. Annesley.
Coulson, I understand, was the manager >f one of the company's mines in Nanaimo. There is the crux of the whole matter in one short telegram, a telegram from Sir William Mackenzie's private secretary to himself, pointing out the iniquities of the union leaders, claiming that the strike was brought about by an unlawful vote, that they knew what was going to happen, that they knew there was going to be an indignation meeting before very long, but that the union leaders were not going to stand by the men, that they were going to refuse to furnish funds and the men would have to go back to work; the men would next apply to Ottawa-and now, Sir, you have got to the bottom of the whole thing and if they failed at Ottawa. ' the union is

dead and the labour trouble is ended.' From that day forward there never was any possibility of these people winning at Ottawa. They had to lose at Ottawa, and when they did lose, the Mackenzie and Mann interests were triumphant, the union was dead, and the labour trouble was ended. When you read that telegram, which I am surprised was given us, and take in conjunction with it the mild manner in which the Minister of Labour has treated this question, I think you will have the key to the whole situation. It is only another illustration of the old rhyme:
Tender-handed stroke a nettle,
And it stings you for your pains;
Grasp it like a man of mettle,
And it soft as silk remains.
If the Minister of Labour had grasped this matter like a man of mettle, he would not have the trouble he is having here tonight. It is all very well for the hon. member for Nanaimo to say that conditions had reached such a stage about a year afterwards that they could not be helped. If the minister had not sat idle for about eight months, that condition of affairs would never have existed.
I have read down to the 17th of November, and according to the report given to my leader, not a finger was lifted for five months. The minister allowed the strike to go on and thousands of men to be idle in British Columbia, secure in the fact that he was doing the bidding of Mackenzie and Mann. He simply sat tight and did the bidding of the interests. These people lost at Ottawa, the strike was ended and the union was dead. I am not here to defend labour unions or international unions. I do not know whether I am fortunate or unfortunate, but there is not a member of Parliament of the whole 231 who has as little to do with labour unions and labour matters as I have.' I know there are two or three small railway unions in my constituency, and so far as I know they are all international unions. They get along amicably with their employers. There was a difficulty about a year and a half ago with the checkers. The Minister of Labour refused to do anything. He refused to recognize these men and to give them a board because the Canadian Pacific railway did not want him to, and it was only after the hon. member for Rouville '(Mr. Lemieux) and myself brought the matter up in the House that the Minister of Labour got a move on; and within one week after the matter was ventilated in the House, the minister did not have any trouble in
. 1
arranging a settlement with the Canadian Pacific railway; and the checkers' strike was over, and the men of my town, at least, all went back to work. That is all I have had to do with labour unions, and therefore I cannot be successfully or honestly charged with discussing this matter in order to make-political capital out of it. It matters nothing to me, personally, whether the mines in British Columbia win or lose, but it does matter to me as a Canadian citizen and as a member of Parliament that the Minister of Labour, who was appointed and is paid for the purpose of looking after the interests of labour in Canada, should sit down, fold his arms and do the bidding of the big interests, while the miners and their wives and families starve. He does not care so long as he is able to carry out the instructions of his masters, the corporations. That appeals to me, that is my business,, that is the minister's business, and that is the business of every man in this House.
I said also, that it looked to me on the surface as though there were an unholy alliance between the Canadian Northern Railway Company and the British Columbia Government. I want to come to that for a few moments. I find on page 12 of the report of Mr. Price, the commissioner, that at the very inception of this trouble the labourers did everything they possibly could in order to have this matter settled according to law. In the first place, remember the labourers did not claim that they had struck. I am only giving the version of many people which has been referred to in this House many times. The miners claim that two of their members had been discriminated against because, acting in the performance of their duties as a committee of miners, they had reported the existence of gas in one of these mines. They claimed that one gentleman, Mottishaw, I believe, was removed from work in a particular mine, that he was politely crowded out, and was given no further work to do. He went to another mine, the Cumberland, got work, and, after three days, was politely crowded out of that. Because these men had reported the existence of gas in one of these mines they were simply refused work and discriminated against.
That was the cause of the trouble. 1 have here a very instructive little pamphlet issued by the Rev. John Hedley, pastor of the Haliburton street Methodist church in Nanaimo. I know the minister received a copy of it, because I find in the corres-

pondenoe a letter from this reverend gentleman to the minister, and also an acknowledgment of the minister to himself.
I do not know who Mr. Hedley may be, excepting what I see in this small circular, and what I learned from the report of Mr. Price. I find that he was a gentleman of sufficient importance to be entitled to give evidence before Mr. Price, and a summary of his evidence is given in the report brought down in response to the request of my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid. Laurier). I find that this gentleman states that gas had been found in these mines a great many times, and that there had been a fearful loss of life as the result of it. He said that in 1884, in the Wellington, mine, 23 men were killed; in 1887, at Nanaimo, 180 men were killed; in 1888, at Wellington, 50 men were killed; in 1904, at Extension, 17 men were killed, and in 1909, at Extension, 33 men were killed. That is a terrible toll of human life resulting from this one particular cause.
On account of that, legislation was passed by the British Columbia legislature giving the miners the right to appoint committees to investigate this condition of affairs. The miners, acting upon their legislative rights, their individual rights, their civil rights, and their rights almost as British-horn citizens, in order to protect themselves, sent this committee down into the mine to investigate it, and they came back and reported the existence of gas. Because of that report-at least so the miners claimed-these .men were simply fired out of their jobs, they could not get places, they were refused work at their ordinary avocation and practically the only kind of work that they knew anything about. These are the facts as given to us here. Then as a protest against that, and in order to discuss the matteT, they took a holiday. When they came back next morning they found a notice posted up saying: Get your tools out of this mine; you can only come back if you will sign an agreement to work under certain conditions for two years. If they had signed this agreement the union was dead. There is no use in trying to get away from that fact. It seems to be the intention of the mine owners that this union must be killed-1 do not know why. You never can tell me that Mackenzie and Mann, Who have been working with international unions for the last twenty years, who know all about international unionism, who have
members of international labour unions on every railway they own in Canada, and who have members of international unions probably on every street railway they own in Canada, were determined to drive out this union because it happened to be an [DOT]international union. That is all nonsense. The reason must have been that they were determined to drive out this union because they believed the union would be a benefit to the miners and possibly inimical to their financial interests. There is no other possible conclusion to come to, and there is no use in my hon. friend the minister reading, as he did three weeks ago, and as his friend the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) did this afternoon, an article written by a member of the international union who afterwards came to British Columbia-I refer to Mr. Farrington-about wanting to organize British Columbia to protect the American miners from competition. There is no use in my hon. friend trying to throw any such herring as that across the trail. These international unions are here >and my hon. friend might as well recognize it. These international unions will be in the coal mines of Canada and he cannot help it. Yet he allies himself with vested interests and financial interests in order to prevent them from coming. But they will continue to come and he will have to accept the situation. There is no use of my hon. friend trying to get away from the fact that his fight is a fight against international unionism. He cannot deny it. He may deny it in words, but he cannot deny it as a matter of fact. He cannot make these international labour unions of Canada believe that that is not the real fight that he is putting up to-day. He cannot make the ordinary man who reads believe that the real fight is not a fight against international unionism.
I have no brief to defend or condemn international unionism. I know that as far as my own limited experience goes-and that is of the railway order-international labour unionism has been an unbounded success. There has not been a labour strike that I know anything about in eastern Canada, excepting possibly the fight with the local union in Nova Scotia when, I think, they should have lost, that the international union have not obtained, if not in every case, at least in many cases, in which their demands were not unreasonable, a material victory, thus benefiting the status and condition of the men whom they represented. I believe to-night that had the minister taken a different course, had

the union been helped to go on with their work, had the minister accepted the union, there would have been a much better condition in British Columbia than there is at the present time.
As I say, at the same time the minister was notified, these men notified the authorities in British Columbia. I do not want to take up time toy reading the whole of the letter which was addressed to Sir Richard McBride. It is to be found at pages 12 and 13 of Mr. Price's report. In this letter, dated September 21, and addressed to Sir Richard McBride, Premier of British Columbia, they state in a very moderate and prudent manner the whole cause of the trouble from their standpoint-I am not saying they are right or wrong; I am only saying from their standpoint:
Now, Sir, the information that we desire from you is this: When men are appointed or elected as a gras committee at any mine in this province, and do their duty under the law what protection does the law afford them? Does it prevent the employer or his agents from discriminating against them nr discharging them m case they make a report not satisfactory 'o the management?
Your obedient servants,
' Kobert Foster,
District President.
. G. Pettigrew,
International Board Member.
* David Ervine,
International Organizer,
per George Pettigrew The record is silent as to whether Sir Richard McBride condescended to give an answer to these people. I do not know-the Minister of Labour has not furnished us with the information, if he has it, and if he has not it, he should have it-I do not know whether a reply was given to this by Sir Richard McBride; but we do know that same sort of a board was organized by the British Columbia Government, and this board spent a great deal of time trying to came to some sort of a conclusion. It was called the Royal Labour Commission, and the miners spent about a week in presenting their case before this commission, in the month of February, 1913, which would be four or five months after the unfortunate strike took place in Nanaimo. Therefore, Sir Richard McBride did something, whether he acknowledged the receipt of this letter or not.
I shall read some extracts from the letter of Mr. Farrington, addressed to the deputy minister under date of May, 1913. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that after the general strike was called on the 1st of May, the minister got * busy, very busy. There is fMr. Carve.ll.]
no doubt that he then commenced to write letters, and to send telegrams, and he commenced to see the enormity of the condition of affairs which he had created by his negligence and by throwing himself bodily into the hands of the interests. He wrote to a Mr. White, who was president of the United Mine Workers of America in Indianapolis. Mr. White handed the correspondence over to Mr. Farrington, who was in Canada looking after the interests of the strikers. This letter is of so much importance that if it had not been read and placed on ' Hansard ' by my hon. friend from Maisonneuve some weeks ago, I would have been inclined to read it to-night. As it is already in ' Hansard,' hon. members and the public can read it if they wish to. I only want to refer to certain portions of this letter which deal with the action of the British Columbia Government. Mr. Farrington describes what had been done with the Government, to some extent and with the company. Dealing with the British Columbia Government, he says:
Next we spent from February 19 to 26 inclusive before the Royal Labour Commission, which was created by the provincial Government to investigate labour conditions throughout the province, presenting the miners' side of this controversy and exposing the merciless and thievish practices of the Canadian Collieries Company, so well did we succeed that members of the Royal Commission unofficially informed us that they were convinced of the justice of our position, and promised the undersigned that they would use their good offices in order to bring about a satisfactory adjustment of the existing differences, so that you will know that we had no objections to the aforementioned commission using their influence to bring about an adjustment. There were three letters written by myself, and which read as follows:
I shall read the three letters which follow, to show that these miners did everything which reasonable business men could do in order to have this matter settled by the powers that be, and under the legislation existing. They applied to the British Columbia Government and spent a week before this Royal Commission, and then they wrote this letter:
Victoria, B.C., February 27, 1913. Mr. G. H. Parsons,
Chairman, Royal Labour Commission, Victoria, B.C.
My dear Mr. Parsons:
I trust you will pardon me for writing to confirm my declaration made before your honourable commission in Ladysmith yesterday, and I deem the controversy between the Canadian Collieries Company and the United Mine Workers of America to be of sufficient importance to warrant an immediate report and recommendation by your commission to this particular feature of your work.

If the judgment of your commission is in accordance with mine, I take this means of repeating that your good offices will be acceptable to the United Mine Workers of America, and so far as you may be able to use them to bring ^bout a settlement of this controversy.
Thanking you and the commission as a whole, for the courtesy shown the mine workers during the hearings at Cumberland and Ladysmith, I am,
Tours truly,
Frank Farrington.
Not receiving any answer to that, Mr. Farrington wrote again on the 7th of March, 1913, from Fernie, B.C.:
Fernie, B.C., March 7, 1913. The Hon. H. G. Parsons,
Chairman, Royal Labour Commission, Victoria, B.C.
My Dear Mr. Parsons:
Will you kindly advise me in care of P.O. Box 789, Nanaimo, B.C., as to whether your commission has been able to do anything towards bringing about an adjustment of the trouble at Cumberland and Ladysmith, and as to whether you are doing anything in this connection.	,
Yours truly,
Frank Farrington. ^
Not receiving any answer to that, he wrote, on the 20th March, 1913, for the third time, from Vancouver, B.C.:
Victoria, B.C., March 20, 1913. The Hon. H. G. Parsons,
Chairman, Royal Labour Commission, Victoria, B.C.
My Dear Mr. Parsons:
Will you kindly refer to my letters of February 27 and March 7 and advise me as to whether your commission have done or contemplate doing anything in connection with the miners trouble at Cumberland and Ladysmith? I have some plans of my own, which I expect to bring into use, in order to bring about a settlement of this trouble, which I am holding in abeyance, while awaiting the action of your commission. While I have no desire to hurry the commission I am anxious to know whether you have any plans in connection with this trouble, and would like to hear from you not later than Wednesday, March 26.
Please address me c/o Box 798, Nanaimo, B.C., and oblige.
Yours truly,
Frank Farrington.
After waiting considerably over a month, Mr. Parsons, the chairman of the commission, who had privately informed Mr. Farrington that he was in sympathy with him, and would do something to help him out, wrote this most remarkable document:
Golden, B.C., April 3, 1913. F. Farrington, Esq.,
International Board Member, District No. 12, United Mine Workers of America,
Box No. 798,
Nanaimo, B.C Dear Mr. Farrington:
Your letter of the 20th instant has just reached me, and it is with considerable regret
that I have to state that I know nothing which the Royal Labour Commission can do in regard to the matter referred to.
Yours truly,
H. G. Parsons.
Nothing further was done by the British Columbia Government, not a finger was raised to help in the difficulty; the commission which wanted to make a report in favour of the miners,-I say so advisedly, were refused the right to do so. They were not even in a position to answer the letters; and finally this letter was written, which,
I consider, while couched in courteous language, was certainly an insult to every labourer in British Columbia.
Nothing further was done until after the riot had occurred in the month of August, and blood shed. As has been described, some women and children were turned out of their homes and driven over the hills into the woods, and a condition of affairs existed, which happily had not existed in Canada for a great many years before, and I hope never will occur again. After that, this same British Columbia Government, and I say this advisedly too, instead of doing something to try to mitigate the trouble, were the instrument and means of having some. 400 soldiers and extra police sent to Nanaimo. The labour men were practically decoyed into a meeting in their hall and surrounded by soldiers; were first ordered to march out in file, but eventually got sufficient time to transact business, and were then marched out in the middle of the night, and thirty-seven of them were sent to prison like ordinary criminals, and not given the right of British subjects to have bail under certain conditions. We all know that bail is granted to practically every criminal in Canada where the sentence would not -be more than five years. I am only stating this as a general principle, but it is practically correct. These men were treated, not like Br.tish subjects, not even like Russians in their own country; they were treated more like inhabitants of Siberia than like inhabitants of any other country that I know of on the face of the habitable globe, and treated in this way by the British Columbia Government. If we can believe the information which we are receiving from people in that locality, the grossest partisanship has been exercised by this Government in order to wreak their vengeance upon political opponents and to stand by at least their political and business friends, and some go so far as to say that it is in order to stand by their own financial interests.

I have here a most remarkable letter from a gentleman about whom I know nothing whatever. It was written to me in response, I presume, to something which he read in the newspapers regarding the discussion which we had some three. or four weeks ago on this matter. I read this letter in order to show the condition of affairs existing in British Columbia and the manner in which the British Columbia Government tried to settle this strike. I give it for what it is worth. If the man be not responsible, then it does not hurt the hon. minister. If the man be responsible, it is in my judgment the most terrible indictment I have ever heard in this House of the conduct of any government or of any set of government officials. I did not suppose that such a condition of affairs could exist in Canada, and I do not believe that there is another place in Canada where it could exist. The letter is as follows:
Nanaimo, B.C., February 15, 1914. Mr. Carvell, M.P.,
Ottawa, Canada.
Sir,-I see you are taking- some interest in the affairs of this province. We have had a strike in this locality since September 1912 and in this town since May, 1, 1913, and they were caused by the fault of the provincial government in not carrying out the laws that exist on the statute books in regard to gas in mines, and can easily be proved any time by any unbiased investigation. Crothers and the others the Dominion Government sent out here never tried to investigate, only tried to exonerate the companies and blame the miners. The trouble started in Extension mines owned by McKenzie and Mann. A few years ago an explosion took place in this mine and killed thirty-two men and two days before the mine was reported clear of gas by Government inspector. The mines employ a gas committee of their own and pay them and it is lawful to do so.
