I did not think of that phase of it, but I will certainly read no portion of the letter again which refers to any member of this House. I shall be very particular about that. (Reading):
The two men employed by the men reported gas in a certain place and were discharged for doing so and were blacklisted as well. They went to see McBride and he told them if they had found gas and not reported it they would have been put in jail and he was asked what protection they had for reporting it and he said he could do nothing. Personally I don't think the strike altogether devolves on the miners. As far as I can learn the property is terribly

over capitalized and rumour hath it McBride an 1 Bowser are in on it. The Government has never tried to bring the contending parties together hut they have spent a large amount of the people's money to help the corporation to defeat the workers and have never given the workers any protection, and today you cannot stand two on the streets without running the risk of being arrested. I have talked to men who have been all over the world and they say it is the worst they ever saw. The people of this district are intelligent and law-abiding in so much as this is the largest mining camp on the Pacific and we had our jail closed for years for want of occupants but the crime is in not sending Conservatives to the local House, and one thing I am surprised at is the forbearance of the people that they havn't rose up in rebellion against the British Columbia Government. If they had done this in England, they would have torn the jails down before now. They seem to try to irritate the people to rebellion to have the chance to shoot them down and if they are determined to use Russian methods they will be met eventually by Russian tactics, the bomb, and all the Government investigations have been royal farces. I have given you a brief outline of the situation. If you want any further knowledge on this Question I will be glad to give it. You may think that I am a miner but I am not. Never worked in a mine. I have been in business here over twenty years and have a rating in Duns and Bradstreets. I will state what treatment I received at the hands of Bowser and his lick spittles around here. I was on Nicol street collecting on the 11th of August about 4 o'clock and there was a little trouble between a family who had been receiving over $100 per month relief from the union and had started to scab. The trouble didn't amount to anything but the authorities magnified it. I was standing a little piece away from the crowd talking to another business man, and a constable put my name down and not the other man as he was a good Conservative and I have a list of 40 Conservative business men who were there and none of them arrested, and not one Conservative has been arrested in the whole district. About a week after I was arrested, searched and thrown into jail, brought up next morning for a hearing and sent up for trial without bail. I could have got fifty thousand dollars bail if necessary. About. thirty of us were chained together and put between double rows of soldiers and marched through the streets to the station and taken to-Victoria jail to wait jury trial. We waited there about two months and then thought too-long to wait for assizes and came up to elect for speedy, trial, chained together again and. marched through Victoria streets and in the train if you wished to use toilet you had to take the other man with you as the police would not loosen handcuffs. Waited some time about three weeks for speedy trial and then saw Government was railroading the men to jail and. through a technicality were allowed to re-elect for jury and chained together again and marched through the streets of both towns again and thrown in jail again, and when any one tried to give us any fruit, tobacco or any food, men and women were brutally assaulted by soldiers and police after being in jail three months. I was let out on my own recognizance of a thousand dollars and not tried yet. They are doing all they can to irritate people to rebellion to get the chance to shoot

people down and justify this roaring farce. It was never necessary to put troops in here, and they want an opportunity to shoot up to justify them. The other day I was standing on the sidewalk that I paid for on my own store, that I paid for and was ordered away by the law and order gentry special police, the scum of Vancouver and Victoria, but any one that votes the Conservative ticket in British Columbia can commit no crime, but if he don't, its a crime to move or a crime to stand still, and the British Columbia Government in my opinion is the most [DOT]corrupt and corporation-owned Government on the American continent to-day.
Yours respectfully,
(Sgd) I. Hodgkinson,
Nanaimo, B.C.
I shall be pleased to send this letter over to my hon. friend the Minister of Labour if he wishes to read it. I am reading from a copy, but I have the original.
After reading a letter of that kind from a white man in Canada, I do not care who he is or what he may be, if any man has any British blood in him, it will boil; if he has any blood in him at all, it will boil at treatment such as that by a government of a citizen. Yet my hon. friend sits back and smiles complacently. He says:	I
have Mackenzie and Mann behind me; I can do as I have a mind to and what can you do about it? My hon. friend will have another tribunal to face, and he will find that he is not yet through with his conduct in the Nanaimo strike.
I have here another short piece of evidence which I wish to read, and this again is from the Rev. John Hedley. I find it on pages 15 and 16 of the pamphlet which he sent out, and I commend it to the earnest consideration of my hon. friend:
The men who were apprehended in such numbers were flung into the Nanaimo jail. Although innocent until proven guilty-many have since been discharged-they were treated as criminals. Given no opportunity for bail except in case of sickness, confined three in a cell 0 x S feet, the only sanitary arrangement a bucket placed in the cell and emptied once a day, dysentery rife, yet no trace of disinfectants ; food meagre and poor; brought to and from the jail to the court house by armed soldiers and special police; manacled by handcuffs when brought to and from Victoria; confined eight or nine weeks before trial, such is the treatment accorded them by British Columbia justice.
Contrast this with the treatment given by the Government to the strike-breakers. They have had full liberty, properly housed and fed and cared for in every way. These are the transients of many nations, while the strikers are citizens of the city and district. Since then the authorities have manifested a mania for making arrests. Men have been arrested on the most doubtful and trivial charges of intimidation and picketing. Many of these charges have not been sustained, yet the victims of this
tyranny must go to jail whether innocent or guilty. The result is a general breakdown of all regard for British law or justice. As far as the miner can see the law and the administration of the law exists solely for the protection and help of the mining companies. All loyalty to the state must vanish when it is recognized that-the state does not stand for justice or fair-play.
I have given you to some extent the attitude of the Mackenzie and Mann interests and of the mine owners generally, and I have given you some little description of the attitude of the British Columbia Government. Now, a word as to the attitude of the Minister of Labour. He sent the miner.? a telegram stating the law-which, as I have said, they knew as well as he. He then folded his hands and did nothing except to write a few letters; he sat down and enjoyed his salary for five long months, until a general strike was called and 3,500 men were out of employment in Vancouver island. Then he .sent further telegrams, and finally appointed his friend, Mr. Price -and I have nothing to say against Mr. Price, he 'may have been as good for this service as any body else-to go out to British Columbia. But he did not send Mr. Price out to settle this dispute; the hon. gentleman himself will not say that he did. He sent him out to investigate conditions and report, under the provisions of the Inquiries Act. Investigate what? Why, there is not a thing in this report that the minister had not in his office before he sent Mr. Price to British Columbia. The minister simply squandered a few thousand dollars in giving his former partner a nice trip at the expense of the country. Also, he delayed the matter for three or four weeks longer and gave himself a chance to go out there and consult with his friends the mine owners, come back and get away to England. It looks like the most unholy temporizing with a serious condition of affairs that I have ever heard of in a civilized country. He knew the strike had taken place; he knew as much a? he knows now concerning whether it was a lock-out or not. He knew that the trouble was between the mine owners and the union. He knew a general strike had taken place on the 1st of May. He had this report of Mr. Farrington some time in June, before Mr. Price was sent out and before even the Order in Council was passed appointing him. For the Order in Council appointing this friend of the minister was not passed until the 23rd of June, and the minister had the Farrington Teport in his hands a

week or ten days before that. He had, I believe, privately and personally, the side of Mackenzie and Mann on this question, because they had been here and he had seen them. He knew everything that Mr. Price could find out; but simply for the purpose of delay he appoints his friend to go there at a splendid salary and find out what he already knew. This done, he tells us he could do nothing more.
Well, Sir, the point has been referred to by my hon. friend from South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll), and so I shall not take up much time in discussing it; but the minister had it in his power to settle this difficulty in twenty-four hours if he had wanted to do so. I make the statement here that the Minister of Labour could have settled this strike simply by lifting bis hand.	He makes the boast, as
his friends in this House and his newspaper supporters make the boast- and will do it again, at the next election, before every railway audience in Canada-that the Minister of Labour wielded the big stick over the Grand Trunk railway company and made that company take back men whom they claimed they ought not to take back, under the settlement effected between themselves and the late Government. The Grand Trunk railway claimed that they had carried out their contract, but the Government took the contrary view. And when the Grand Trunk railway came to this Parliament for legislation which they really wanted, the Minister of Labour sat back in his seat with the most cynical smile I have ever seen on his face-and that is saying something-in effect saying: You will get no legislation from this Parliament until you settle the strike and put these men back. The Grand Trunk had to put the men back, and they did. The men were reinstated, and the Grand Trunk got their legislation-' you pays your money and you takes your choice.'
Now, let us see what the position was in regard to the Nanaimo strike. The minister's friends, Mackenzie and Mann, said they were bankrupt-I do not believe it, I have no idea that that was the case at all; and I did not believe it then any more than I believe it now. But they wanted sixteen or seventeen millions of our good money to help them over a financial diffl-' culty, and they said to the minister and his friends: We delivered the goods in the last election; we stood by you, and we want you to contribute sixteen or seventeen mil-
lions. Does the Minister of Labour say that he could not have wielded the big stick then? Do you think that Mackenzie and Mann, merely to persist in refusing to recognize a labour union in British Columbia, would have foregone seventeen millions of cold cash when they and the Bank of Commerce wanted it so badly? Why, you have only to state the proposition to show its absurdity. Yet the Minister of Labour tells us: The strike had reached a point where we could do nothing to help the settlement of it. The Minister of Labour's friend, the hon. member for Nanaimo, says: I have honestly come to the conclusion that it cannot be settled. This legislation in favour of Mackenzie and Mann did not go through until some time early in June. The general strike took place on the'1st of May-one month before. The representatives of Mackenzie and Mann were hanging around the corridors for fully a month, fairly begging the minister and his friends for that sixteen or seventeen millions. They said they had to have it, The case was so urgent that, as the minister knows, his supporters had to be fairly whipped with scorpions to get them in here to support that legislation. He had to go so far as to promise an increase in indemnity-which he did not give them. He had to resort to tactics which no minister in a Canadian Parliament has ever resorted to before in order to press a Bill through Parliament. But he tells us that he could not -say to Mackenzie and Mann:	Call off
that strike. Well, I do not believe any man who makes that statement. Now, I challenge the minister, and I hope he will answer and tell us why he could wield the big stick over the Grand Trunk when they only wanted legislation, but could not do it over the Canadian Northern railway when they wanted millions of our money, which, I have no hesitation in saying, they were not justified in asking for. That is practically the whole thing in a nutshell.
I started by making the statement that the suspicions were in favour of the theory that there was an unholy alliance between the minister, Mackenzie and Mann and the British Columbia Government. I have given you nothing but the documents brought down by the minister himself except this letter of Mr. Hodgkinson from British Columbia. I have simply discussed this matter from the record, and have drawn what in my judgment is a reasonable conclusion, the only conclusion that can honestly be drawn from the documents. I hope the minister will do this House the

justice to answer, and not only this House, but the people of this country and the miners of British Columbia especially who have been suffering untold misery, suffering a condition of affairs which, I believe, has not existed before in a British country in the last hundred years. I ask the minister to tell this House and these miners why he did not apply the same methods in the case of Mackenzie and Mann in June, 1913, when they got an enormous amount of our money, which he had applied to the Grand Trunk railway only the year before when they simply wanted legislation. I ask him to tell why he sat idly by for five er six months and did nothing; why he did not attempt to bring on a board. No doubt, he will tell us again: Oh, a judge in Quebec has said, I am afraid there is something wrong with your statute; I am afraid that if you interfere you may get in wrong, be called down and make yourself a laughingstock. But, Sir, I tell you it is no laughing matter to the poor miners and their wives and children in British Columbia. It is no laughing matter to the labouring people all over Canada that the minister has seen fit to do nothing. It is a matter of supreme importance, a matter of so much importance that I think it is the duty of this Parliament, before one dollar of Supply is voted, to see that the minister answers these questions, and absolutely clears up the imputations against the good faith and bona fides of the Department of Labour as administered by him.

Mr. Speaker, I have not taken up much of the time of this House since I have been a member of it, nor did I intend to take up any time in connection with this particular affair until I listened to the remarks of the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell). I did not intend to address the House on this question, because I do not profess to know the merits of the case in dispute. It is true that I live in British Columbia and very close to the scene of this trouble. I have tried to follow the dispute through the press of the country; I have tried to gather the usual fair-minded idea of the merits of the two sides; and yet I am far from having any definite or decided opinion as to the merits of the case.
Since I have occupied a seat on the floor of this House I have tried, in my own weak way, to get an idea of the workings of the minds of some of the members of the House. I have been particularly interested in following the views of the hon. member
for Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell); and I may say that it is hard for me to-night to keep within parliamentary language in telling you what I think of the state of mind that he must be in when he can make the insinuations and the charges, without decent foundation, that he does in this House against the members and the minister. If there is an insinuation against the character of any man in this House or out of the House who is his political opponent, spoken of in the press or talked about on the streets, he delights to come on the floor of this House and to put it forth as if it were a fact. He seems to wallow-yes, that is a good word for it-in insinuations, innuendo and general charges against the characters of othet people and other governments and all those who do not agree with him. He does not seem to even look for reasonable proof of his statements-somebody says no proofs. He does not need proof. All he wants is a report to be passed upon. In my boyhood days I was always taught to keep an eye on the man who did not have a clean mind, and I have tried to govern myself along those lines; and the man who is always ready to accuse his neighbour of some wrong doing, you can take my word for it, has not a clean mind and you had better look out for him.
This gentleman talks about an unholy alliance between the Conservative Government of British Columbia, Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann, and the Minister of Labour of this Government. He brings as proof of that a letter that has only to be read to any intelligent person to stamp it on the face as being the most distorted view that could possibly be given of
10 p.m. any ordinary occurrence. He tells us that the Conservative Government of the province of British Columbia are to blame-for what? For sending the troops to	Nanaimo to
protect the lives and property of good, respectable, responsible people. The troops would never have been .sent to Nanaimo had it not been for the fact that before they were sent there, these miners, led by irresponsibles, carried off their feet by the teachings of these irresponsibles, committed the most dastardly crimes it was possible to commit, burned and destroyed property, turned men and women and children out of their homes, attempted to commit murder by throwing bombs into the houses which men, women and children were occupying. Red riot was running through that country; and yet this man.

seeking to gain a little political advantage for his party, has the hardihood to say from his place in this House that the provincial Government was wrong in protecting the lives and properties of respectable persons. I care not what the situation is as far as the dispute is concerned to-day; but I do know, in all fairness, that there are two sides to every dispute. It may be in this instance that the men were right in the first instance and the company wrong; but the actions that necessitated the calling out of troops were certainly wrong.
The Government of British Columbia have tried to handle the affairs of the province in a just and fair manner to all interests concerned. That they have done so is evident from the fact that every time they have appealed to the country they have come back with a larger majority. The people of that province are well content with the present Government, not only in their past actions, but in their actions in connnection with this particular matter; and I do not believe the Government would hesitate, if necessary, to appeal to the people on that particular question. When the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) attempts to prove an unholy alliance between Messrs Mackenzie and Mann, the Conservative Government and the Minister of Labour, he has a very hard job ahead of him.
There is no evidence to show that there was any collusion between these different parties other than the communications they are entitled to have in the ordinary way. The miners have the right to put their case before the Minister of Labour; so has the company, and each party has the same rights :so far as the local Government is concerned. This country is not governed for the labourites, nor is it governed for the capitalists. The Government is, and ought to be, for all classes; all interests should be protected, and I believe that is what both these governments are trying to do.
The hon. gentleman held up his hands and told us that the Minister of Labour could have settled this dispute in 24 hours that when Mackenzie and Mann came here foT $17,000,000 he could have used the big stick and said:	You cannot have this
money until the coal strike is settled. Does not the hon. member know that the Canadian Northern railway and the Dunsmuir Collieries, Limited, are two distinct institutions; does he not know that the latter is a British flotation owned and controlled absolutely in the old country? It is true

that Sir William Mackenzie is identified with that institution, and possibly carries a large amount of its stock, but the control of that company is in the old country. It would be a nice thing for the Minister of Labour to say to the manager of the railway company:	If we are going to assist
your company, you must go out and take another company in which you are personally interested by the throat and insist on their settling some dispute that is going on. The hon. gentleman is not fair. I do not believe that his mind will allow him to be fair. I believe that in the very near future we will all agree that the very best plan has been followed and that there will be no honest criticism of 'either Government for the methods they have pursued. The strike, so far as the people of British Columbia and the people of Canada are concerned, is something we all regret very much; but let us be men enough to discuss the situation in a fair manner and without attempting to gain a party advantage by appealing to either the labour vote or any other vote in this country.

In the views which I have the intention of presenting to the House upon this question I will endeavour to follow the advice of my hon. friend who has just taken his seat, and try to present those views in a fair manner without endeavouring to obtain any party advantage in doing so. The proposition which is before the House is that the House should affirm:
That the whole conduct of the Minister of Labour in regard to the claims and rights of the coal miners on the island of Vancouver was marked by persistent negligence and absolute indifference and deserves the censure of this House.
This is certainly a very severe indictment against a minister of the Crown, because the minister is here charged with nothing less than dereliction of the duties that are cast upon him in the office which he has accepted. I have to say, after having looked over the record, that in my judgment the indictment is well founded, and I want to give my views to my hon. friend. I shall endeavour to do so in a temperate manner, so that he can answer, if he chooses to do so, the objections which I have to raise against his conduct.
I do not charge my hon. friend with having failed to prevent a strike, but I charge against him that he took no steps whatever to stay a strike which he knew was impending. It was his duty as minister of the Crown to use every possible means to pre-

vent a strike which he knew for weeks and months was to take place; and the charge which I bring against him is that during all those months he took no effective steps to prevent what he was sure would come unless something was done by him.
It appears from the record that some time in the month of September, my hon. friend heard that there were labour troubles in British Columbia. At once he took a step in which he showed diligence, and if that first step had been followed by similar diligence, he would not find himself in the painful position in which he now is. He addressed this telegram to Peter McNiven on the 7th of September:
My attention has been drawn to newspaper despatches announcing the occurrence of coal miners' strike at Cumberland mines. The Industrial Disputes Investigation Act provides means for possible settlement of all matters in dispute by reference to an impartial board of three members, on which company and workmen concerned may each have a representative of their own selection. Law does not compel acceptance of board's findings but forbids strikes or lockouts pending inquiry under severe penalties. In present case requirements of the Act do not appear to have been satisfied, and I am desirous of learning particulars of dispute by telegram without delay. Department will furnish any further explanation of industrial disputes law which may be required, and is to-day mailing you copies of this law and forms of application thereunder. In the event of proper application being made, everything possible will be done to expedite procedure under Act.
T. W. Crothers,
Minister of Labour.
An answer was received by the minister the following day in these words:
There is no strike declared at Cumberland mines. The company have openly discriminated against men who were taking an active part in union organization. They also refused to meet a committee of men. The men decided to take a holiday, after which the company gave orders for men to take their tools out of the mines.
J. J. McAllister.
The answer which was at once given to the minister upon his very proper offer of service was that there was no strike at the time, but that the company was openly discriminating against the men. If you want to know what was meant by the men in stating that they were being discriminated against, we find it in a letter which followed the telegram I have just read, and which was addressed to the minister by Robert Foster (president), and John McAllister (secretary), on the 3rd of October, but we find it still better in a letter dated September 21, 1912, and addressed to Sir Richard McBride, by a committee of the men composed of Robert Foster (district president), 83
G. Pettigrew (international board member), and David Ervine (international organizer). There you will find in a few lines the statement of the real difference between the men and their employers. They go on to say:	*
Some two or three months ago Oscar Motti-shaw and Isaac Portray were elected as a gas committee to examine the mines of said company at Extension and report on the condition of the same, as required by law. During their examination they found and reported gas in five working places. The management of the mines, upon the posting of this report, called on the Chief Inspector of Mines, Mr. Graham, to come to Extension and make an examination of the places in question. This he did and the report of the gas committee was verified. Soon after this the place where Oscar Mottishaw was working was finished and he was refused another place. New men were employed while he was idle, waiting for an opportunity and asking for work. Not wishing to he the cause of any trouble between the management and the men there he finally left and went to Cumberland where, he secured employment, wonting for a contractor in the mines of the same company. He had only worked there three days when the contractor, Mr. Coe, received instructions to discharge him, from the superintendent, Mr. Henderson. Mr. Coe demurred, saying that Mottishaw was a good workman and he had no reason to discharge him, asking Mr. Henderson what reason he would give Mottishaw. Mr. Henderson insisted that he must discharge him, saying that he could tell him that the could not pay him $3:50 per day, the amount he had agreed to pay him, whilst the other men were being paid that amount for the same work. Mr. Coe complied with the request of Mr. Henderson and discharged Mr. Mottishaw.
There was the case of the men. It was, as they stated, that these two men had been charged by their fellow workmen with the duty of examining the mines and that, upon reporting that there was gas, they were discriminated against.

I am very sure my
right hon. friend will be glad if I correct him as to that. It was only one of the two men that was dismissed in connection with the examining for gas; the other was not.

I do not say whether or not the case is as stated; I say that the men stated tftieir case to be as I have presented it to the House. I do not say that their case is so; I do not know. What I do say is that here is the complaint which they made.

I think my right hon. friend will find nothing in that statement to show that both men who were on the gas committee were dismissed. As a matter of fact, Portray, who wrote the report, was not dismissed.
That has absolutely nothing to do with the case.
Yes, it has.

No; that is where my hon. friend has made his mistake all along. These men made their complaint. The complaint was right or it was wrong, it was true or it was not true; but they made the -complaint that these two men, M-otti-sh-aw and Portray, who had made the report, had been dismissed, or rather, that they had not been given work. These men had been at work -at certain places and when they had finished their jobs they were not given any further work to do. My hon. friend says that Portray was not dismissed, Then, this is my answer to my hon. friend: It was stated to him that these -men had been dismissed, that 'they had not -been fairly dealt with by the company. I know that the company has stated -all -along that these men were not improperly treated. I know it was stated that Portray was not dismissed at all, but that he was not given work. Here was the statement of the -company on the one side, and here was the statement of the men -on the other side. What was the duty of >my hon. friend under su-ch circumstances? He said to-day that he should take the version of the company that these men were not dismissed. I say his duty was not to take the statement of one or the other. The great mistake he made from the start was not to order an investigation right away and see who was right -and who was wrong.
I do not pretend in this m-atter to speak with any feeling at all. I shall put the case -chronologically as it appears to me, and the charge I make -against my hon. friend is, in the words of thi-s motion, that he has -acted with persistent negligence, with -absolute indifference; and the very statement that he makes when he interrupts me now is evidence of what is affirmed in this motion, that he has acted with want of diligence and with indifference. If my -right hon. friend had understood his duty, -as he should h-ave understood it, he would have endeavoured, at the very first moment -when there was -an issue between these men -and their employers, to find out the truth; -and, in pursuance of this obvious duty, to send -an agent to the spot and have an investigation made. If my hon. friend had done that, what would have been the result? His efforts might have been unavailing; but at all events he could have said to-d-ay: I have done the best I could; I have failed, but, at all events, n-o man could do m-ore.

But will my hon. friend tell us that he has done everything that he should have done, that he has exhausted every means possible? After the moment when he became -aware of this issue between the men and the company, his obvious -duty was to see who was telling tlhe truth- the -company or the men. What were the facts? Where was the truth? That was the first duty which was incumbent upon him.
But there was another thing he should have done, it was his obvious duty, and I must express my surprise that he did not do it. When he wrote to the company, as he did, and when he received the answer which I have just mentioned, was it not obvious to him that he should send one of his officers to try and bring these two parties together ? When the minister found himself faced with the position of affairs that existed at the Cumberland mine, it was his duty to send a conciliator to the spot to try and bring the men and the company together. He finally did send Mr. Acland, his deputy minister, to the Cumberland mine and to Nanaimo. When did he send him ? He sent him in September, 1913, twelve months after he first received notice of this trouble. It was only then that he thought he should send Mr. Acland. Why did he not send him sooner ? Instead of waiting for one year to send Mr. Acland in order to endeavour to bring the two-parties together, after there had been bloodshed, after passions had been wrought to the highest pitch, if he had sent him in the month of Septmber, or October, 1912, is there not reason to believe that he would have achieved some results ? I will not be so unfair as to hold my hon. friend responsible because the strike was not prevented, but I cannot hold him guiltless of negligence and indifference to the rights of these men.
I said a moment ago that I did not desire to bring any passion into this debate. I am a party man, I do not conceal that fact, but I prefer to fight this battle rather upon the ground of policy than upon personal grounds. In the long course of my political career I do not think I ever entered personally into an argument against an opponent. In this case it is not because I want to make a point against my hon. friend; but It seems to me that he has a duty to perform since he has accepted the position which he now occupies. His duty is to watch, and to watch closely, every difficulty that may arise between employer and employee, and to endeavour to prevent the trouble from continuing. If

the hon. gentleman had been as diligent as he ought to have been, the result might have been different. But what did he do? He allowed the month of November to pass; he allowed the months of December, January, February, March, April to pass, and all that time he must have been aware there was seething trouble in Nanaimo. And yet he did nothing. I heard the hon. gentleman say this afternoon, in answer to my hon. friend from Sydney, that there was some correspondence with regard to this in the month of October, and that the last cor espondence that took place was in the month of November. Nothing was done by the department, even by way of correspondence, after November.
What did my hon. friend do later on? He waited until June or July, and then, he repaired to British Columbia, and there is not a report even of what he did there. Then he left to take a holiday. I would be the last man to find fault with him for taking a holiday, but does the minister believe he was discharging the duties of his office when he took a holiday at a time when bloodshed was occurring in British Columbia? On the contrary, it seems to me that the minister should have been there all the time, night and day, watching, to prevent, if possible, the unfortunate things which occurred.
He told us he appointed a commissioner. I find no fault with the selection of Mr. Price, as commissioner, but I do find fault that the commission he gave to Mr. Price was not at all with reference to this trouble. Mr. Price was not charged, in the commission which the minister gave him, to make any attempt towards a settlement of the trouble; the commission issued to Mr. Price was simply to make a general inquiry, with a view to amending the law, so as to prevent the recurrence of disputes of this character. The whole commission to Mr. Price was, to make a general survey and a general report, which he has done.
There is the case against the Minister of Labour. He has failed altogether to do anything which was commanded by his position, in order to bring these two parties together and prevent a strike. What could be the influence; what could be the reason which actuated the Minister of Labour? He started very well, but he stopped very short.
Now, I would not say that the Minister of Labour was prevented from acting because the Canadian Northern Railway Company was to be found on the other side 83i
of the case, or because my hon. friend found out in British Columbia that the owners of the mine were the Canadian Northern Company. My hon. friend from Kootenay (Mr. Green) stated that there was no evidence of collusion between the Canadian Northern Company and the Minister of Labour. I do not say there is. The hon. gentleman stated also that the Canadian Northern Company were not the owners of that mine; that Sir William Mackenzie may have had an interest in it, but that the .mine belonged to some parties in England. I do not know how that is, and I care not. I do not think it matters much who are the owners, but I know that the correspondence with regard to this case was carried on, not with Sir William Mackenzie, but with the Canadian Northern Company, and the evidence is that every letter in the record from the owners interested is to be found written upon the paper of the Canadian Northern Railway Company.
And headed Mackenzie and Mann.
I will not go so far as that.
One of the letters certainly is.
I will take the case just as I find it. There is so much in the correspondence that something may have escaped my eye which has not escaped the eye of my hon. friend (Mr. Carvell).
It is there, all right.

It has been pointed out this afternoon that a letter from the Deputy Minister of Labour was addressed to Mr. D. B. Hanna, third vicepresident of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, and that is significant. Here is another letter in the correspondence; it has been read, but in view of the statement made by my hon. friend from Kootenay, I think it will bear reading once more:
Ottawa, September 27, 1912. Re Disturbances in Coal Mines at Ladysmith and Cumberland, B.C.
Dear Sir,-With further reference to the industrial troubles in the coal mines controlled by your company on Vancouver island, concerning which the department has exchanged telegrams with you, the minister, I am to state, is particularly desirous of having, without delay, your company's statement on the subject, and would be obliged if the same could be

forwarded immediately. Statements received by the minister go to show that work has ceased at Ladysmith as well as Cumberland, the alleged ground being discrimination against membership in' the local union, but the department is not fully informed as to this. The situation is one in which it would appear probable that an application would shortly be received for a board of conciliation and investigation, and the minister has thought your company might desire to take action which will render unnecessary the establishment of such a board. Can you kindly arrange to have a statement expressing the company's view forwarded to the department, so that it may be placed before the minister on Monday, the 30th.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd) F. A. Acland, Deputy Minister of Labour.
D. B. Hanna, Esq.,
Third Vice-President,
Canadian Northern Railway,
Toronto, Ont.
That letter as will be seen is addressed to
D.	B. Hanna, Esq., Third Vice-President, Canadian Northern Railway, Toronto, Ont. Again, on the 6th of October, another letter is addressed by Mr. Acland to Mr. Hanna, as follows:
Ottawa, October S, 1912.
Dear Mr. Hanna:
I am enclosing the documents you left with the Minister and myself this morning, relating to the Vancouver island difficulties. I have had copies of the documents made.
Tours very truly,
(Signed) F. A. Acland.
D. B. Hanna, Esq.,
Third Vice-President,
Canadian Northern Railway,
Toronto.
I read these letters in answer to the statement made by my hon. friend from Kootenay (Mr. Green), to the effect that there has been no collusion between the Canadian Northern railway and the minister. I do not say there has been, but I say: whatever may have been the circumstances, whatever may have been behind the scenes, Mr. Hanna was asked again and again to give information as to the nature. of the difficulties between the company and its men, and though a promise was made day after day, yet no information was given; at all events, no information is to be found in the correspondence, as having come from the Canadian Northern Railway Company.
There is another statement here which is very significant. It has been said with reference to this, that the Canadian Northern Railway Company induced the Minister of Labour not to grant an inquiry. I do not say that, but I do say that the Canadian Northern Railway Company made a suggestion of that kind to my hon. friend,

and the statement upon which I found my charge is in a letter which is to be found in the correspondence from Mr. Annesley, secretary of Sir Wm. Mackenzie, and which reads:
Canadian Northern Railway Company, Offices of the Third Vice-President,
Toronto, Ont., October 7, 1912. Translation of message to Sir William Mackenzie:
Coulson Wires:
Replying to my telegram of the 10th, I did not state that two weeks ago our miners were prevented from voting on resumption work by local union president, who destroyed ballot boxes and also threatened men . Local union officials realize error in not giving thirty days' notice before striking and also in not having consulted international union and are trying to avert responsibility. International union repudiate action and will not support strike morally or financially. Conditions very quiet but we expect men very soon to hold indignation meeting and return to work repudiating union entirely. Union appeals to Ottawa their last resort. If unsuccessful union dead and labour trouble ended.
(Sgd) F. B. Annesley.
How did that telegram find its way to the Department of Labour? Somebody must have sent it there, and who could it be but the man to whom the telegram was addressed? There is no covering letter. We cannot find out how it came there, "but the suggestion is there contained and the words are very suggestive:
Union appeals to Ottawa their last resort. If unsuccessful union dead and labour trouble ended.
And there was no investigation and no action taken by the Department of Labour. Unfortunattly the trouble was not ended; it was only commencing. The charge w'hich I have to make against my hon. friend is, that he did not act at all. I do not charge against him that he acted upon the suggestions contained in that telegram. The record is bad enough without making any charge at all. I simply lay the facts before the House and let them speak for themselves. More than this I have not to say against my hon. friend, but I thought that I owed it to him that, before he spoke, I should tell him how that question strikes one who, although an opponent, does not want to have any cause for prejudice against him. It would, however, be hard for my hon. friend to give to the House any justification which would absolve him of the negligence and of the indifference charged to him by the motion now before the House.
Before I take my seat, I want to say a word about the strikers. It was very properly stated that the men had been guilty

of very serious offences. Far would it be from me to defend them from the offences which they committed against the law. The law was violated in a very serious manner; but who is the man who would charge them with it? These men were goaded to madness. They implored in vain; they expected in vain the intervention of the department. Nothing came. When their blood was hot, when reason perhaps was not as strong as it ought to have been, when bad treatment had goaded them into a condition which ought not to have existed, they resorted to violation of the law, which must be condemned. Nothing can justify the excesses which took place; but if nothing can justify these excesses, there are circumstances where there may be excuses for the offences, and I have to say that in my humble judgment the men who are in jail to-day for committing these offences are not half as guilty as those who by supineness goaded them into committing them.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. W. CROTHERS (Minister of Labour):
speechtext:
I shall refer for a moment to my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) who has just taken his seat. I did not think that he would intentionally misrepresent conditions, but the fact is that he very grossly misrepresented conditions in Vancouver Island. Before pointing out the particulars in which he has misrepresented the facts, I wish to congratulate him upon the progress that he has made in the direction of taking a deep concern in the interest of the workingmen of this country.
My right hon, friend was the head of the Government in the year 1906 when a strike occurred at Buckingham, about twenty miles from this city. The attitude taken by my right hon. friend's Government at that time was that they would take no part in that strike or attempt to settle the dispute between the men and their employers unless requested by both parties to do ,so.

There was bloodshed too,
wasn't there?
Mr. CROTHERiS: In order to prove that, I shall read a letter from my hon. friend the Minister of Labour at that time. The men at Buckingham, on the 26th day of September, 1906, wrote to the Minister of Labour of that day asking him to intervene to effect a settlement between them and their employers. This is a letter from the then Minister of Labour, Mr. Rodolphe Lemieux, which shows conclusively the attitude taken by my right hon. friend's Government at that time on the question of intervention:
November 2, 1906-
My Dear Weir:
This letter was written to the Hon. W. A. Weir, Minister of Public Works and Labour, Quebec.
Re Buckingham strike. I have to thank you tor your letter of the 31st ultimo, and for your kind promise to send copies of the several reports made by Mr. Marois. With regard co what you say as to the report of our inspector, I would state that this matter was not investigated by any officer of the Department of Labour. The procedure of the department, in most of the cases with which the department has had to deal has been to intervene only where both sides have been willing to accept the department's friendly offices. In this case the employees concerned asked the department to lend its good offices towards adjusting the difficulties existing. The department at once communicated with the company offering its mediation, but met with such a flat refusal that it was thought no good would come through intervention.
And there was no intervention, and the result was that, although the men requested intervention on the 26th of September, 1906, a riot occurred on the 18th of October in which three men were killed, a large number injured, and the militia went there from Ottawa and remained there for some time in order to protect the interests of the people.
That was in 1906, and I charge my right hon. friend with having neglected his duty at that time when there was a strike within a stone's throw of the seat of Government. When the men asked his Minister of Labour to go down and intervene and try to settle the matter, his Government said: We can do nothing unless both parties ask U3. They refused to go there at all, and the result was that three men were killed and several seriously injured.
Does my hon. friend not know well that the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act wa? not placed on the statute book until the year after that?

Of course I know, and I am a little surprised-no, I am not surprised that my hon. friend from Pictou should ask such a question. My hon, friend from South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) pointed out a day or two ago that the Conciliation Act was in force from the year 1900, and it was under the 'Conciliation Act that my right hon. friend could have directed an inquiry. The Conciliation Act was passed in 1900, seven years before the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act was passed.

Is my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) satisfied?
I will let my hon. friend (Mr. Crothers) know when he gets through.

Since my hon. friend (Mr. Macdonald) has seen fit to interrupt, perhaps I might call his attention to something that occurred in Nova Scotia, his own province, when a strike was on there, and when the Government of the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) which the hon. gentleman supported, was in power. On the 7th of July, 1909, the Minister of Labour of that Government received the following telegram from Mr. M. J. Gillies, M.P.P., Glace Bay, N.S.:
Five thousand employees Dominion Coal Company on strike here. Situation looks serious. Important that you get here immediately and try to effect a settlement.
What did my hon. friend from Pictou write to that Minister of Labour? His letter was dated that same day, the 7th of July:
Det me congratulate you upon the fact that you were not troubled with an election and that you have got into the saddle without very much trouble.
I doubt very much whether that congratulation was absolutely sincere.
I have just been talking on the phone with our mutual friend Alex. Johnston, and our joint opinion in regard to the situation in Sydney is that at the present stage it is not wise or prudent for you to come down or take part in the situation. There was a rumour in Sydney that you were to he asked to come down-
And the hon. gentleman proceeds to head him off.
-and I am writing as a result of my interview with Johnston, to say that I think for the present that you should not come down. We will advise you a little later in the matter-
No politics in this, of course.
-and if it can be possible for you to produce any result you can depend upon our judgment in the matter.
But he could not wait for the letter to reach the Minister of Labour, and was afraid he might act in the meantime. So he sent a telegram:
I am wiring you in case any request has been made.
Then, we have the reply from the Minister of Labour, dated the 13th of July, 1909. This letter shows what a change has come over the spirit of their dream during the last few years. The right hon. gentleman thinks there ought to be intervention

at once. But in 1909, he was quite ready to see his Minister of Labour supported by the hon. member for Pictou, take no action whatever. This is his letter to the hon. member for Pictou:
I have received your letter of the 7th instant confirming your wire to the effect that it was Alexander Johnston's wish and yours that I should not take any part in regard to the situation at present.
Of course it was in the interest of the men, in the interest of the country, that something should be done, but this Minister of Labour took this advice from the member for Pictou and Mr. Alexander Johnston and did not send anybody to the scene of the strike.
Though it was not my intention to intervene in any way, I am glad you wired me promptly.
So, though there were five thousand men on strike, and though the Minister of Labour of the late Government received word from a political friend that the matter was looking very serious, he accepted the telegram from the hon. member for Pictou that he and Mr. Alexander Johnston thought it better that he should not go to the scene of the strike.
Is the hon. member for Pictou the representative of Glace bay?

No, Mr. Johnston represented that district, if I remember well. Nowj I would like to ask the hon. member for Pictou, who is present on this occasion, whether there is any truth in the statement that in those days he desired the striking miners of Nova Scotia to be imprisoned. I would like him to answer that question.

Mr. Speaker, when
this hon. gentleman gets through answering the resolution presented by my hon. friend from Maisonneuve-
Oh, oh.
-and answers it like a man on its merits, without accusing other people in regard to other matters, I will discuss this question with him.

The hon. gentleman
refuses to say whether there was or was not any truth in the statement that he desired the striking miners in those days to be arrested. I am not prepared to prove further than this, that he insisted upon the Government prosecuting these men for having gone on strike. Here is a letter from him dated the 14th of August, 1909:

The strike situation in Nova Scotia has been summarized in this way, that in Inverness, the strike practically does not exist. There are some men who are not working, but these men are not necessary to the adequate operation of the mines. In the Dominion Coal Company's works, from which I have just returned, the company are rapidly increasing their output and the men are only being kept out on strike, at least a great portion of them, by the usual stories which the resources of the United Mine Workers people supply to them, of the fact that the company are going to settle and various reasons are given for this from week to week. I do not doubt at all that the company will be successful there, and there may be a break very shortly. I think that the men will eventually realize that the company will not on any terms settle their compromise. The Springhill situation is one I am not advised about and is really very serious. The situation at Inverness and the action of the United Mine Workers is a direct and absolute defiance of the provisions of the Conciliation Act, and I think it would be a great mistake if the department itself-not the company or any outside party or person-[DOT] did not proceed against the United Mine Workers people who came out on strike in disregard of that Act. I notice by the press that inquiries are being made by the department with reference to the circumstances, and I am quite sure that you will find the facts to be that the strike is one which is in contravention to the Act. And can assure you of my fullest support in so doing if you should arrange to have these proceedings initiated. It seems to me that the effect of the department proceeding against this infraction of their own law would be a very good move in Nova Scotia.
This is the man who last week showed so much concern for the striking miners out in Vancouver, so far away; but when they got near to where he lives he insisted on the Government prosecuting them and sending them to prison for striking. He did not quit with one letter. I shall read several letters to show that he insisted, time and time again, on the Government sending to prison these men who had gone on strike in Nova Scotia, and still he gets up before us now and manifests great concern for the miners away out in Vancouver island.
At the present time public opinion is strongly against the strikers and against every one who is connected with them, and there is no question about their desire to have the matter speedily dealt with by a strong hand. In the event of your taking any proceedings, I would suggest that the matter be put in the hands of some recognized lawyer of ability-
Oh, oh.

Does my hon. friend mean any insinuation by that?
Mr. CROTHERS. (Reading):
Some recognized lawyer of ability.
My hon. friend would have filled that
bill, because he is a recognized lawyer of ability.
That insinuation is worthy of the hon. gentleman.

I thought that was a compliment rather than an insinuation. The letter goes on:
-such as Mr. Roseoe, of iientville, who has been acting for the Militia Department.
So that we had the militia down there looking after the interests of the public; and yet my hon. friend would not allow the Minister of Labour to go to Glace Bay because his supporters, Messrs. Macdonald and Johnson, did not want him there just then for political purposes.
In the event of your taking any proceedings I would suggest that the matter be put in the hands of some reognized lawyer of ability, such as Mr. Roseoe, of Kentville, who has been acting for the Militia Department and making some investigations in that matter. I should be very glad to hear from you in regard to this matter.
(Sgd.) E. M. Macdonald.
An answer was sent to that letter by the Minister of Labour. It was dated the 17th of August, 1909. It is from the Hon. Mr. King. It is a very lengthy letter and I shall read only portions of it.
With regard to the administration of the criminal laws generally it is, as you know-*
Fancy my predecessor instructing my hon. friend from Pictou in the law.
-it is, as you know, administered by the provinces. No department of the Dominion Government and no officer of the Dominion acts as a special agent for the Government in giving effect to its criminal legislation. Under the circumstances, it would seem that there should be very special reasons for a departure
11 p.m. in the case of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act and one of these reasons, it would appear to me, should be that the regular course of procedure having been tried has been found insufficient or ineffective. Where a province, a municipality

I hope my hon. friends will listen to this, because here is an enunciation of the attitude they took with reference to the enforcing of the laws passed by their own Parliament, and I may have occasion to refer to this when my right hon, friend comes to refer to some other Act. Here are the general principles laid down by the Government, led at that time by the right hon. leader of the Opposition.

where a province, a municipality, a company, an individual or a set of individuals, any one of which may be adversely affected, is not prepared to lay the information against any individual or set of individuals who are acting in

a manner prejudicial to their interests when the law as it stands affords them this measure of redress, it is difficult to see just why the federal Government, which is the least remotely affected of all-
The Government not affected at all by the strike of five thousand people; not affected at all when the militia are called out in Nova Scotia to protect life and property; and my right hon. friend's Government, through his Minister of Labour, announces that the Government has nothing to do with anything of that kind; it is for the individual.
Where a province, a municipality, a company, individual or set of individuals, any one of which may be adversely affected is not prepared to lay the information against any individual or set of individuals who are acting in a manner prejudicial to their interests, when the law as it stands affords them this measure of redress, it is difficult to see just why the federal Government, which is the least remotely affected of all, should be expected to take the initiative in entering a prosecution.
That is what the hon. member for Pictou wanted them to do.
When the means of redress are so ready at hand. The most obvious inference to be drawn where no information is laid, is either that interests are not being seriouslv affected, in which case it would be a mistake for the Government to attempt prosecution; or that in the circumstances known to the parties the law has not been violated, in which case, of course, a prosecution would be of no avail.
Still my hon. friend from Pictou was not satisfied with that and he sent another letter; he knew more about it than the Minister of Labour at that time. This is the letter sent in answer to that on August 20:
Hon. W. L. M. King,
Minister of Labour,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Mr. King:
X have your favour of the 17 th and note its contents. I am very much obliged to you for the frank way in which you have written me in regard to the matter. I do not agree with you altogether, that the main motive of the men who struck at Inverness was not openly to defy the Act. The idea has been generally circulated by the Opposition people

You see the Conservatives were in opposition then, they are on this side now.
The idea has been generally circulated by the Opposition people that the Act was of no force or value and whether they desire to openly defy the Act, or not, they were certainly very regardless of it. The United Mine Workers is still maintaining an attitude of hostility.
These are the men he is weeping over now in Vancouver island.
The United Mine Workers is still maintaining nn attitude of hostility to the company, and the
[Mr. Crothers.j
men who compose the organizations are still out. Mr. Moss, one of the district officers, is still in Inverness conducting the strike. It does seem to me that on the whole, it would be in the best interests of the order and of the public if the Government should take steps, so that the mining men should understand that the United Mine Workers' men should understand that this Act is a serious proposition and is not one that is to be openly disregarded. I do not think you need at all fear as to any injuries resulting in the subsequent working out of the Act and I am quite satisfied this would be the proper course to take from a matter of standpoint.
They have here ' a matter of standpoint.' I do not know what that means.
I am going to Sydney on Saturday and will write you after my return from there.
Yours faithfully,
E. M. Macdonald.
But he was not satisfied with that. He was very persistent in his desire to have the striking miners sent to jail. Here is a letter dated August 25, to Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, Minister of Labour, Ottawa.
Dear Mr. King,
With reference to the matter of action in regard to the situation in Inverness, I have made careful inquiry with reference to the facts and find them to be as follows: At a meeting of the United Mine Workers at Inverness at which the two organizers were present when the question came up, as to whether there should be a strike or not, the organizers told them that they would not recommend them to strike, that it was a matter entirely for the local union, but if they did strike they would stand behind them, and give them financial assistance. I have inquired into this matter carefully and that is the information that Mr. McGillivray the manager gives me. What is more, they have carried out their promise by giving assistance as Joseph B. Moss, one of their council is on the ground superintending the giving out of relief. I do not know any better evidence that there could be of section 60 of the Act than this, for the representatives of the United Mine Workers to encourage emp Oyees to go or continue on strike, than by saying ' If you do strike, we will pay yqu.'
Section 60 prohibits the aiding or encouraging of an illegal strike. It has been held in Nova Scotia that giving support to miners on strike by a union is illegal, and comes within section 60, so that my hon. friend from Pictou in writing that letter said in substance to Mr. King. Under section 60 those United Mine Workers' officials are doling out flour, meat, pork, and butter to the striking miners. That is a violation of section 60. Do your duty as Minister of Labour and imprison these men for violating the Act. And yet he is so much concerned about the welfare of the poor struggling miners on Vancouver island. He goes on:

Under the circumstances I really think that the department should vindicate this law by taking some action. The general feeling in Nova Scotia among all classes outside of the coterie of Conservative politicians,-
He could not leave them out.
-who are backing the United Mine Workers is that some legislation should be enacted in the approaching session of Parliament which would prevent the possibility of American strikers coming into Canada and engaging in strikes such as they have done in Nova Scotia this year.
His proposition is that if the law is not strong enough to prevent officials coming into this country from the United States it ought to be amended, and yet he comes here and talks about the poor miners. He goes on:
I think that the logic and basis of such legislation is unanswerable. The feeling among our people is very strong on the subject. I can arrange to give you any information you desire-	-
My hon. friend from Pictou not only wrote the Minister of Labour that he ought to prosecute these people but he said: ' I will be a detective for you and give you information.'
-further, with reference to the matter, and trust that you may see your way clear to take some action.
1 think that is about the fourth time he wrote the Minister of Labour urging him to take such action.

Will my hon. friend be good enough to send me over those documents.
Mr. CROTHERlS: I will send you copies.
I assumed my hon. friend was reading from copies, if not I would not have asked him.
I am reading from the original.
Put them on the table, then.

'My hon. friend from Nanaimo read this afternoon a portion of an article written by Frank Farrington, vice-president of the United Mine Workers. Hon. members will remember that portion of the article that was read this afternoon by my hon. friend from Perth, pointing out the superior quality of the coal of Vancouver island, and north of Vancouver island as far as Prince Rupert, and pointing out that these mines were being tapped preparatory to supplying coal for Atlantic ports as well as for ports on the Pacific after the
opening of the Panama canal, and pointing out that it would be impossible for the [DOT]mine owners and miners ot the United States to compete with the mine owners of Vancouver island because of the superior quality of our coal. This article was sent to the United Mine Workers of the United States by Farrington because, as he says in the beginning of it, the people of Canada understood the situation but the United Mine Workers in the United States did not; so he proceeds to enlighten them. There has been some doubt cast upon this article by some hon. gentlemen this afternoon. It appeared in the United Mine Workers' Journal published in Indianapolis and dated the 27th of March, 1913. Let me read a paragraph or two that have not been Tead in order that you may see the exact situation.
May I ask the minister if that is signed by Mr. Farrington as a contribution to the Gazette?

It is in the United Mine Workers' Journal under this caption: 'The situation in Vancouver Island, by Frank Farrington, in the United Mine Workers' Journal, March 27,	1913.' I
would ask hon. gentlemen to remember that he is addressing the United Mine Workers of the United States, and I want to satisfy you that the steps that he was taking were directed in the interest of the mine owners and mine workers of the United States and not in the interest of the mine owners or mine workers of Canada.
May I ask my hon. friend if this argument that he is now making is in justification of the fact that he did not interfere and did nothing?

I have confidence in the intelligence of my fellow-members to whom I am addressing this argument, and I am sure that they will judge it properly. In this statement he says:
So that it is not beyond reasonable conjecture to expect that within a comparatively short time we will find this coal bidding- for markets on the Atlantic seaboard as well as on the Pacific coast. This feature in itself would not be so bad if there could be an interchange of competition but that cannot be, for the reason that the mu:h superior quality of this coal will always bar outside competition from its own zone.
The duty devolving upon the United Mine Workers of America-
Mark you, upon the United Mine Workers of America.
-because of this condition,-

Because coal produced on Vancouver island will take the place of coal produced in Washington .state and other parts of the United States when the Panama canal opens, and because of this condition we must organize.
The duty devolving upon the United Mine Workers of America because of this condition, is to organize Vancouver island and adjacent territory, raise the standard of employment and act as a balancing medium in the establishment cf equitable competitive mining rates.
Not because the people of Vancouver island are suffering, not because the mine workers of Vancouver island are getting low wages, or are being ground down, but because of this condition to which I have just alluded. Mr. Frank Farrington would balance things up. Mr. Frank Farrington would tell the mine owners on Vancouver island how many hours in a day or how many days a week they shall keep their mines open. He says that the United Mine Workers of America will 'act as a balancing medium in the establishment of equitable competitive mining rates.' Then he proceeds:
This will be a herculean task, but it must be done, or we must suffer from inevitable competition, and the job-
J-o-b.
-can be easier done now than after the task gets bigger.	.
Snuff them out now before they get stronger and bigger! We should do it now in the interest of the mine owners and workers of the United States !
Recognizing the seriousness of this condition and being desirous of protecting the interests of our membership, as well as being anxious to extend assistance to the men employed on Vancouver island-	[DOT]
This is the first time we have heard of Vancouver island.
-the international executive board decided to expand the power and protection of the organization to the island. In keeping with this decision a district convention was held in Nanaimo during the month of November, 1911, and a district organization was formed.
Keep in mind all the time: 'Because of this condition we must organize Vancouver island.' They called a meeting in November, 1911, organized, and the strike followed ten months afterwards.
As hon. gentlemen opposite have referred to the letter that this man Farrington wrote to me, while I am not prepared to admit that every statement in it is true,
I am prepared to accept it as against
[Mr. Crothers.l
himself. Here is what he says, as shown on page 681 of 'Hansard.'
