I am reading from this letter. I will read it from the original if it is any better. He says:
I have just been favoured with a copy of the official report filed with your department by Royal Commissioner Samuel Price, who, I understand, was appointed in accordance with an Act of the Dominion Parliament to investigate the coal-miners' strike now existent on Vancouver island. Because of my having charge of this strike from its inception, I think I can discuss the report with a reasonable degree of assurance-
Order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I will have to ask the
hon. gentleman to desist, or read something else, because the privilege cannot be refused to another if it is allowed now in violation of the rule.

I am not reading part of a speech; I am reading a letter written by this man Farrington. He says that he had charge of the strike from the inception. He comes over here in November, organizes the union, has charge of the strike from its inception; and he says further in that same letter, and I want to especially call the attention of hon. members to the statement, that at the time of the strike the coal mines in Vancouver island were as safe as human hands could make them. These are the words that he uses in that letter prior to the strike. While we have hon. gentlemen opposite trying to lead this House to believe that there was something wrong, that there was gas or something in the mine, we have their leader stating that prior to the strike the mines of Vancouver island were as safe as human hands could make them.
There is this further. It will be remembered by those who have read Mr. Price's report that it sets forth two or three extracts from a report made by the commission in 1903, composed of Justice Hunter and the Rev. Mr. Rowe, my predecessor, Mr. King, being secretary. I believe that Mr. King wrote the report. But this man Farrington, in this letter, because Mr. Price quoted two or three paragraphs from that report, proceeds to say that the report of the commission of 1903 was

virulent in tone, unwarranted by the facts and injurious to the miners of that time.

That is the way he criticises the report of 1903, made by Chief Justice Hunter and Rev. Mr. Rowe, Mr. Mackenzie King being the secretary of the commission and writing that Teport, as I believe.
Now, Sir, I have given you some evidence which will enable you to appreciate and to understand what occurred after that. Everything that occurred on Vancouver island, I submit, must be read in the light of that communication, and interpreted by that communication. What do we find? We find in September, 1912, a report in the newspapers that some 1,500 men had gone on strike at Cumberland. My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition will persist in the statement that men who were on the gas committee were dismissed.
I did not say that at all.
You said that the men said so.	*
Exactly.

That is not so. I do not say for one moment, and I would not for my right hand accuse my right hon. friend of making a misstatement intentionally; I do not believe he would do so, but he is under the impression that the men said these two men were dismissed. There is nothing in the correspondence to show that; there is nothing in the letter read by my right hon. friend to show it.
Read it.

I have read it. What they said was that Mottishaw and Portrey were members of the committee, and they go on to show that Mottishaw was dismissed. But Portrey never was dismissed, and they do not say he was. I challenge my right hon. friend to find anywhere where the men themselves say that Portrey was dismissed. The right hon. gentleman will find them saying that they were discriminated against, but without naming anybody.
It is scarcely worth while going through all the facts again. What is the complaint? No one has come down to any particulars as to a complaint. Is there a single hon. member opposite, who has spoken on this matter, who has suggested that I should have done anything that I did not do? We have had some very remarkable statements during this debate, and I feel very much like taking my colleagues in this House into my confidence, to the extent of making the confession that there are some
men utterly incapable of a generous thought, of an honest impulse, or of an unselfish motive. Moral degenerates themselves, their vision discerns in others nothing but depravity.
The fact is that in Vancouver island, as in Nova Scotia, the issue between the companies and the men was recognition of the United Mine Workers. My right hon. friend became very warm this afternoon in advocating the case of the poor strikers out on Vancouver island, but what was the position taken by his Government, when they were in power? He will find it expressed by my predecessor, the Hon. Mr. King, in ' Hansard ' of February 24, 1911. My hon. friend from Westminster (Mr. Taylor) was discussing the Nova Scotia mine troubles, and he said:
At Springhill, as I understand it, the matter at issue was the recognition of a union, and the question raised by the hon. member for Halifax was whether or not this department has made any endeavour to secure recognition of the union by the proprietors of the mine where the trouble occurred, or whether the department took the opposite view and stood behind the mine owners in declining to treat with the men; on that basis I think we ought to hear from the minister with regard to that point.
My hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Car-vell) to-night lashed himself into paroxysms of eloquence because this Government did not insist upon the company recognizing the United Mine Workers of America. Did not you all hear him? He repeated it over and over again, and he will perhaps dream about it to-night. Mr. Taylor, the member for New Westminster, put to the Government of that day, in 1911, through their Minister of Labour, the question, whether they had done anything to induce the company to recognize the union. And what was the answer of Mr. Mackenzie King, the Minister of Labour:
Mr. King: I have no hesitation in saying that the recognition or non-recognition of a union is something to be entirely left to the parties themselves. The department would not be justified in asking employers to recognize the union.
And yet my hon. friend from Carleton says that I ought to have brought pressure to bear upon the company to recognize this union and get the matter settled. The Government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, through its Minister of Labour, declared that the department would not be justified in asking the employers to recognize the union, any more than in asking the employees to take any particular stand against the employers who failed to recognize the union. Mr. King said:	That is a matter to be left to the

parties themselves. Mr. King utterly refused to do anything, where the issue is the recognition of the union. But my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has reformed since then, and he thinks the Government ought to compel the mine-owners to recognize the union.
I know very well that the great majority of trade unions in this country are international in character, affiliated with like organizations in the United States, and to that I make no objection, speaking generally, and I never did. This organization, the United Mine Workers, is one of that kind. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) will be interested to know what happened in Nova Scotia, with reference to this particular organization. There were three boards appointed there, under the Industrial Disputes Act: one presided over by Judge Chipman; another presided over by Judge Wallace, another presided over by Judge Longley. I want to read short extracts from the judgments of these gentlemen, as to the United Mine Workers of America:
The most important question before the board was that of recognition of the United Mine Workers by the company. Here there is no question of agreements, it is purely a matter of policy. The United Mine Workers claim the right to approach the management by a committee, as is done by the Provincial Workers Association. The company refuse to recognize that right. The principle reason, however, why the company refuses to recognize the United Mine Workers is that they are practically a foreign organization having dangerous and menacing powers under their constitution.
My hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) approved of that judgment; my hon. friend from Cape Breton South (Mr. Carroll) backed up the judgment of this board, as well as the judgment of the other boards, to which I will refer later.
It is true that the United Mine Workers is international in membership, but the principal executive officers and the great bulk of the members reside in the United States. The company points out that this has a very serious bearing on the coal trade of Nova Scotia, inasmuch as the American operators are making serious inroads in the Canadian markets.
It appears in the evidence of Mr. Duggan that since 1906, sales to the St. Lawrence markets of American bituminous coal have increased 531,000 tons. As the St. Lawrence trade forms the chief market of the Dominion Coal Company, anything that tends to interfere with it would naturally affect the interests both of the coal company and the miners they employ. The board considers this objection of the coal company a very grave one, because with one foreign organization controlling the miners, labour difficulties in the United States would almost certainly lead to complication in Nova Scotia. If through labour troubles in the United States a market

opened up there for Nova Scotia coal at profitable rates, pressure would undoubtedly be brought to bear on the miners in Nova Scotia to prevent exports of our coal to the United States. It is true that the United Mine Workers is recognized in western Canada-
It means in the Crowsnest.
-but there the conditions are different because while Nova Scotia mines are finding it increasingly difficult to hold their own against the United States coal in the St. Lawrence trade, the Canadian mines of the west not only hold their own market, but in many cases can aford to export to the United States notwithstanding the duty. Another and most serious objection to recognizing, the United Mine Workers arises in connection with certain clauses in their constitution. One clause of that constitution states that local unions shall be composed of miners, mine labourers and other workmen, skilled and unskilled, working in and about the mines, except mine managers, top boss, and persons engaged in the sale of intoxicating liquors. Under this rule every man except the superintendent and manager of the mine is eligible for membership in the union. This the board considers to be a dangerous and unusual rule and not in accordance with the custom in Great Britain and other mining centres. It is also in conflict with a rule of the Dominion Coal Company, a special reference to which is made in an earlier paragraph of this report. But the most objectionable clause in the constitution is as follows :
* The international officials shall at any time they deem it to the best interests of mine workers in a district that is idle, for just and sufficient reasons order a suspension in any other district or districts that would not in any way impede the settlement of the districts affected, provided that such action would conserve to the best interest of the United Mine Workers of America.' This rule makes it quite possible for the executive of the Mine Workers, whose head office is in Indianapolis, Indiana, to proclaim a strike in Nova Scotia if they considered it to be in the interest of the United Mine Workers as a whole. Inasmuch as all the dominating interests of the United Mine Workers are centered in the United States, it seems clear that the policy of the organization would be governed by the interests of the mines there. Consequently it is not unreasonable to anticipate that on some future occasion, although labour conditions in Nova Scotia might be satisfactory, it would be to the interest of the United Mine Workers as a whole to proclaim a strike in Nova Scotia. That is a power which in our opinion no foreign body should be able to exercise over our industrial interests in Nova Scotia.
The Chairman of this board was Judge Wallace, one of the ablest men in the province, appointed by the Liberals. (Reading):
The board considers that the coal company is amply justified in refusing to recognize any organization that could exercise such a dangerous and continually menacing power.
Yet my hon. friend from Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell) says that we ought to have taken up the big stick and compelled the

mine owners in Vancouver island to recognize this union. (Reading):
Foreign officials sitting in Indianapolis should not have the power to decree that Nova Scotia miners, even when without a grievance, must stop working, and thereby cripple a great Nova Scotia industry.
That is the opinion of Judge Wallace. The [DOT]other two judges in the other two cases, Judge Longley and Judge Chipman, both held that this question of the recognition of a union was not a matter that could be properly considered under the Industrial Disputes Act.
While all this trouble was going on in Nova Scotia, while the right hon. the leader [DOT]of the Opposition was Prime Minister of Canada, his Minister of Labour sent his deputy to Nova Scotia to do what ? To intervene to try to make a settlement between the company and the men ? No; he was positively instructed not to intervene; he was instructed to go and look around and report conditions. My predecessor was afraid of taking a stand against either the workers or the owners. He wanted to ride two horses at the same time. I have in my hand a report made by the deputy minister at that time, and you will find on page 24 this language:
The officials were disposed to negotiate with the company if any opportunity had been found-	'	t	i
That is, the officials of the men. They actually were ready to negotiate.
-and insisted that if they could only get together there was no doubt of their being able to reach an agreement.
What does Mr. Acland say under instructions from the Government of tihe day led by the right hon. the present leader of the Opposition? He says:
I was asked to ascertain whether the companies would see a committee composed only of former employees-
Not including any representatives from the United States and not to be considered as a representative from the United Mine Workers.
I was compelled to reply that my instructions would not permit of my intervening even to this extent, and did not approach the company on the point.
My hon. friend says that the first thing I should have done was to intervene. Yet he as head of the Government of that day sent an officer to Nova Scotia instructing him not to intervene. The officer's instructions were so positive that he says he had
not a right to ask whether the company would receive a committee of their own men or not. Yet hon. members opposite and the right hon. leader of the Opposition find fault with us for doing what we did.
What had we to deal with on Vancouver island? We had the issue created by Mr. Frank Farrington, the man who was there at the inception of the strike, the man who engineered the strike, saying that the difficulty could not be settled except through the officials of the United Mine Workers of America. My hon. friend from Carleton said that Mr. Price did not see Mr. Farrington.
I never said so.

Well, I will take it back; but some hon. members said so this evening. Mr. Farrington saw Mr. Price in Vancouver before he went over to Vancouver island. Mr. Farrington was seen and interviewed by Mr. Price in my presence, so that we got his attitude from the beginning. His attitude was that the strike in Vancouver island could not be settled except through the officials of the United Mine Workers of America. He went to Vancouver island, to Victoria; we saw the representative owners of these mines, and they said: We will never recognize the United Mine Workers of America if these mines be closed for forty years. I believed them. There was the issue. My right hon. friend, when was in power, said: We will have nothing to do when the issue is recognition of the union. Yet 'he lashed himself into warmth to-night because I did not hurry out to fix up a settlement when the issue was the very same one which he refused to deal with in any manner whatever, although he had the Conciliation Act to work upon before the Industrial Disputes Act was passed.
We sent word at once when we heard there was a strike. The deputy minister went to Toronto to see the representative of the Canadian collieries to find out what their attitude was. We saw those men in Ottawa. My hon. friend from Carleton seems to think that it is a great offence to see Sir William Mackenzie about a matter of this kind. I am proud to say that I had the opportunity of talking face to face with Sir William Mackenzie and his vice-president, Mr. Hanna, with reference to this very matter, and I found out from them directly what their attitude was.
Why did you not give us that information?	[DOT]

I am giving it to you now. It was verbal. I saw these men in this city, and the deputy minister went to Toronto to see Mr. Hanna. I speak subject to correction-and got his viewpoint. Their position was:	We will
not recognize the United Mine Workers of America. And they have stood to that. And if what my right hon. friend and his Government said when they were in power is correct, you can do nothing when that is the issue. Yet the right hon. gentleman waxes eloquent, he almost takes me under his wing and attempts to coddle and to pity me, for not doing that which he refused during his term of office to do.
Well, they proceeded to work the mines at Cumberland and Extension, and in a short time they had an output of about sixty per cent of the normal. It has been represented here this evening, and was said a week ago, that men were brought to Vancouver island from England by means of misrepresentation. Of course, I was not in England and do not know what was said to these men. But I do know that I instituted an inquiry in the city of Vancouver through the immigration agent there. Mr. Malcolm Reid, on this question. Five of these men stated under oath that no deception had been practised on them, that they were told that there had been labour troubles at Cumberland, that some of the men who had been on strike were returning to work, that other men wern coming from other places and that the output had reached sixty per cent of the normal; And knowing the facts without deceit or misrepresentation, they came to Vancouver island, and remained there because they had found things better than had beeD represented to them in England. It is only fair to say that a number of these men, when they reached Winnipeg, were taken in charge by representatives of labour there and persuaded not to go on to Vancouver island. Two bunches of them came out, one in advance of the other. The second bunch were induced not to go to Vancouver island. They were taken charge of by the labour people. And it is said that when some thirty-seven or thiTty-eight of these men were under the protection of the labour people who were housing and feeding them, they did sign a paper declaring that misrepresentations had been made to them in England to induce them to come to this country. I do not know whether that is so or not, but as I have said, five of them under oath before
Mr. Reid stated that there had been no misrepresentation whatever.
My right hon. friend says over and over again that I must have known that the strike would spread. How should I have known that the strike would spread? I had every reason to believe that it would not spread. Why? Because all the other miners in Vancouver island were working under agreements, one of which had two years and four months yet to run, one had five months, and one had seven months. These agreements covered all the other miners except those who went out on strike in September. They are set forth in this report of Mr. Price's. I have no doubt that my hon. friend from Carleton and my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition have read these agreements. Yet the leader of the Opposition says that I ought-to have known that all these men would go out on strike about the first of May. I had every reason to believe that the men would live up to their agreements. And I am proud to say that the great majority of the miners of Vancouver island desired to live up to their agreements. Take the leading company outside of Cumberland, the Western Fuel Company, doing business in Nanaimo and employing fifteen hundred men. Of that total number only 240 belonged to this union. But this minority, by the use of the word 'scab' and 'blackleg,' and by a circular sent out as a result of the activity of this man Farrington, chased the other 1,260 out of the mine. I showed to the House the other day the-dodger that was circulated. They would not allow the men to take a vote. Here it is: ' General strike.' I saw a copy of this when I was in Nanaimo-a long, narrow dodger, as red as blood. And those who did not want to strike had called a meeting for that evening to discuss the situation. Notwithstanding that call, this is what this strike dodger said:
General Strike. After having- consulted the managers of the different collieries around Nanaimo, the parties signing themselves as a joint committee have decided to call a meeting at the Princess Theatre at 7 p.m.
While not opposed to meetings of the miners, we beg to inform all employees in or around the mines that a strike has been declared by the United Mine Workers of District No. 28, and endorsed by the National, and will continue until such time as the operators of this district enter into an agreement with the United Mine Works of America. Ballot or no ballot any one going to work in these mines will be branded a scab.
So the declaration was: 'We have called a strike'-that is, Frank Farrington called

a strike in pursuance of his conspiracy as set forth by himself in his articles. It meant: We must get possession of the mines of Vancouver island, we must get control of this valuable property, ' ballot or no ballot.' This dodger was issued under instructions from Frank Farrington, as may be seen. From the 16th of September, 1912, until the 1st of May, 1913, I had no reason to suppose, as the leader of the Opposition would attempt to lead members of this House to think, that a general strike was being arranged for. I am surprised that my right hon. friend should make a statement of that kind. I had every reason to believe that the men who had entered into these three separate agreements would carry out their agreements. I had every reason to believe, and to know, that the strike at Cumberland was not effective, and that the output was growing day by day. And what is the condition of Cumberland to-day ? There are more men there than they can find work for, output larger than ever. At the Western Fuel Company, the output is 700 tons a day-nothing like it was before the strike, but it is growing. The strike is over in Vancouver island.
No one deplores the conditions in Vancouver island more than I do. I regret very much that so many reasonable, decent and intelligent men in Nanaimo and other places were whipped into submission by this foreigner from Seattle-and I have no objection in stating that fact. By the judicious -though that is hardly the word-use of the word ' scab,' 240 men drove 1,260 out, and so all this suffering has followed. I am told-and I believe it came out in the evidence the other day on the trial of Angelo-that this Angelo who led the riot in Ladysmith, was a paid agent from Indianapolis, that he went about the town pointing out the houses that were to be burned, and twelve of them were burned, as he directed. Dynamite was thrown into a man's house and his arm blown off. And yet we have gentlemen on the other side of the House championing the contention that the militia should not have been sent in there to maintain law and order. I say I deplore the fact that so many innocent men and so many innocent women and children have suffered by this conspiracy of Frank Farrington's in the interest of the workers of the United States and the owners of the United States and not in the interests of the men in Canada. I say that has been brought about by Frank Farrington in the interest of foreign conditions. It has been a failure. A great many people
have suffered. The provincial Government took charge of this matter. It was not up to us, as my predecessor said in the letter I read here a few minutes ago; it is up to the province to administer the criminal law. They undertook to maintain law and order in Vancouver island. These men are being tried under the protection of judges who were Liberals before they were appointed to the bench, men who were appointed to the bench of British Columbia by hon. gentlemen opposite; and yet they come forward and say that these men will not get justice from the public officials whom they appointed. I have no such idea of the judges in British Columbia. I have the highest regard for the judges in this country, whether former Liberals or Conservatives. I am proud to know that in this country a man who is appointed a judge rises to the occasion.
Why do you talk about their being appointed by the Liberals if you are so high and lofty about it?

It removes any objections that you may have as to the manner in which they are treating the men who are being tried by them. They are under the protection, at all events, of these judges. Every judge in Vancouver island who has had anything to do with this matter was appointed by the Liberal Government and was a Liberal before he was appointed, and I have no doubt whatever that he is meting out justice. I quite agree with the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Shepherd). I have talked to the Minister of Justice about this thing. I am in favour of liberating these men where there is no evidence of an intentional desire to commit such offences as I have referred to. I quite understand that in the excitement, a number being gathered together in a crowd, men might do things without thinking of their consequences. But for the leaders, the men who went down hours before the burning began and pointed out the houses which were to be burned and those which were not to be burned, I have no sympathy. I think that they should be made to know that when they set their feet on Canadian soil they set their feet in a country where law and order will be maintained at any cost.
I do not propose to take up much more time. There have been a great many base and discreditable assertions and insinuations made by some gentlemen who have addressed the House, and I think the hon. gentleman from South Cape Breton (Mr. COMMONS
Carroll) is the biggest sinner in that regard. I think he is the man who said that Japanese and Chinese and thugs and aliens had been brought into this country to take the places of the white men who had ceased work in the mines.
I say so still.
There is no evidence whatever.
Read your report.

My report does not
say anything of the kind. My
12 p.m. report says there were a number of them working in the mines. That is not wAat the hon. member for Cape Breton said: he said the Japanese and Chinese and thugs and aliens had been imported into the country to take their places.
Correct.

And that is not true. There are Japanese and Chinese working in the mines at Cumberland. I have been told that they have been working in those mines for twenty-five years. They have to get certificates before they can go into a mine to work, just as a white man has. They got their certificates, they went into the mines and they earned their money, I hope.
A great deal has been said about the Foster letter, and I want to refer to it. Foster did write a letter, and I got that letter. Of course, I know that the hon. member for Carleton will not give anybody credit for anything honest or straightforward. That letter was written to me from Nanaimo on the 30th day of September. Nanaimo is sixty miles from Cumberland. I had not the faintest idea when I got the letter from Foster that he had anything, to do with the strike at Cumberland, and he simply says in that letter that the company -I did not know what company, he meant, I supposed some company in Nanaimo-was dismissing men and would not give any reason why, and he asked me whetner there was any means by which they could compel the companies to say why they were discharging men. That is the simple fact.
I did not know he was connected with the Cumberland mines. I got his letter; it went on my personal file; I wrote back that I would look into the matteT, and write him again; and, to tell the truth, I never thought about writing him again. That is the simple fact of the matter. My deputy was dealing with the matter, deal-

ing with both sides. I consulted him. We sent them forms that very day. The very day we got word I sent a telegram that we were sending forms in another letter. We did send forms in another letter, and they never came back. We sent them to Farrington, who wrote back saying he never got them. It is very strange that these things should occur. I think I have a fairly	capable and accurate gentleman in the	office, Mr. Gerald Brown, a particular friend of my right hon. friend. Mr. Brown wrote the letter enclosing the forms. I submit that I did everything reasonable-I did a great deal more than my right hon. friend ever did under similar circlumstances-to bring about peace. I recognize that where the question at issue is the recognition or nonrecognition of a union you cannot do so much, and that was the position taken Dy my opponents. The great majority of the labour leaders whom I have been privileged to meet during the past two years, are men moderate and reasonable, devoted to the best interests of the men they represent, and at the same time having a keen regard to the welfare of the general public; and our immunity from labour troubles in this country during the past two or three years is materially due to the influence of these labour leaders. I appreciate it very much. The great majority, I say; but I am sorry that I cannot include amongst these men the member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville), who is here, and I am very glad to see him. He poses in this House as the only representative of labour. Well, I represent a large number of labour people in the west riding of the county of Elgin, perhaps not so many as he does in Maisonneuve. I am just as proud of the labouring people of St. Thomas, whom I represent here, as he possibly can be of the two or three times as many that he represents in Maisonneuve. He poses as the only representative of labour in this House, and the Liberal press describe him as an independent labour man, which description falsifies his real political character and record. Now, Mr. Speaker, I think the time has come when the mask should be removed, and this man should be revealed to the people of Canada, workingmen and others, in his true light, as a well- defined specimen of that wing of the Liberal party known as the dyed-in-the-wool Grit; and in this respect he rivals my hon. friend from Carleton, N.B., the member for Kings, P.E.I., and the member for Pictou, N.S.

This is the sixth session I have sat in this House, and I have yet to learn of a single occasion when my hon. friend from Maisonneuve voted with the Conservative party. I have noticed that he is just as sensitive to a wink or a nod from the leader of the Opposition as the most pronounced partisan sitting behind his leader. I saw him yesterday having a long interview with my right hon. friend, getting this thing ready. He takes his instructions from my right hon-. friend. The member for Maisonneuve was sitting in this House at the time of the Buckingham disturbance when Sir Wilfrid Laurier refused through his Minister of Labour to intervene. When the House was going into Supply the labour representative in this Parliament, the hon. member for Maisonneuve, did not make any motion. He had a seat in this House when the strikes were on in Nova Scotia, when the Government through its Minister of Labour refused to intervene. He had a seat in this House when the hon. member for Pictou wired insisting that these mine workers should be sent to prison. Yet my hon. friend never suggested that a motion should be made in amendment of going into Supply. My hon. friend from Maisonneuve has never accomplished anything in this House for the working people of this country. I challenge him to show that he has ever accomplished anything in the interests of the working people in the eight years he has sat in this House; and why? Because he has more interest in Alphonse Verville and the Grit party than he has in the labouring people of this country. I had an interview with my hon. friend from Maisonneuve about a year ago. I asked him to come to my room that we might talk over some matters that might be of interest to the working pepople of this country. We had a pleasant interview for half an hour or more. I said to the hon. member: 'If anything occurs to you that can be done to advance the interests of the working people of this country, come to me and I will render you every assistance in my power.' But from that day to this he has never spoken to me about these matters.

The only interview I
ever had with the Minister of Labour was about the eight-hour Bill, and on that occasion the minister never mentioned anything about my coming to see him if I wanted anything for the labouring people of Canada.

Mr Speaker, I have
made one statement; my hon. friend has made another; you can take your choice. My hon. friend from Maisonneuve does not want to benefit the working people of this country. What he wants are grievances. Without them my hon. friend would lose his occupation. He would have to take his coat off and earn an honest living.

I rise to a point of order, and it is that when the hon. minister suggests that an hon-. member of this House would be earning an honest living if he left the House, there is a suggestion that he is not earning an honest living in this House. I submit, with all due deference, that that is language that should not be used in this House.	.
I did not intend to use the word ' honest.' I am only too glad to take it back.
Oh, oh.

I have never understood that it is a dishonourable thing to take back anything you should not have said. What I meant to say was that he would have to take his coat off and go to work. My hon. friend was speaking on this subject in the House about a week ago and he became almost offensive. He made statements that I think are not borne out by the facts. He stated that a resolution was brought before the Trades and Labour Congress asking for my resignation. I am told by gentlemen who attended that congress that it was not concurred in by the committee, and that the motion was simply suggested by a gentleman from Toronto, a photo-engraver. This gentleman wanted my resignation because, while I was acting on behalf of the Minister of the Interior during his absence in England, I refused to recommend the passage of an Order in Council prohibiting all photoengravers from entering Canada from any source whatever. I refused to do that, and that is the top -and bottom of the origin of that resolution. The committee kicked it out, and my hon. friend from Maisonneuve knew that they kicked it out. And yet he had the unfairness to try to lead the members of this House to believe that the Trades and Labour Congress of Montreal had asked for my resignation. With equal colossal assurance he endeavoured to show that I should be dismissed from office and a practical man put in my place. He endeavoured to lead this House to believe that the Right Hon. John Burns, a practical man, was at the head of the Labour Department in



England. The Eight Hen. John Bums has been a member of the British Government eight years, but he never was at the head of the Labour Department in England, and I am sorry that his great representative here did not know that; or, if he knew it, he was attempting to mislead the members of this House. The Right Hon. John Burns has been president of the Local Government Board for some time, but that is not the board that deals with labour questions in England; it is the President of the Board of Trade who deals with labour matters, and since the Eight Hon. John Burns entered .the British Government eight years ago the presidency of the Board of Trade has been occupied by Lord Salisbury, Mr. Lloyd George, Mr. Winston Churchill and Mr. Buxton, every one of them lawyers, I think.
What has been going on in England since this practical man, the Eight Hon. John Burns, for whom I have a great deal of respect, and whom I do not blame at all, has had to deal with strikes? Has he been able to settle strikes in England? There have been more serious strikes in England since he was taken into the Government than ever before. In 1912, there were no less than 40,000,000 days lost through strikes in England; that is roughly one day for every man, woman and child in the United Kingdom. Great Britain has had her great dock strikes, her mining strikes and her Dublin strikes. Every one knows, who has followed labour matters in England, that during the last eight years, while this practical man was a member uf the British Government, there had been more labour unrest in England than there had ever been before. I am not blaming Mr. Burns for it.	.
The hon. gentleman was no nearer the facts when he spoke about the Minister of Labour in the United States, Mr. Wilson. What are the facts with reference to the United States to-day? In Northern Colorado there are 3,500 miners who have been on strike for three years and in Southern Colorado there are 14,000 miners on strike. Yet my friend, Mr. Wilson, a practical labour man and a good man, has not been able to settle the strike in Colorado or in West Virginia, or in Calumet. He has not been anything like as successful in settling strikes as we have been here I think I have satisfied every reasonable man in this House that I have done everything possible to effect a settlement in this case, if I did not follow the example of the right hon. leader of the Opposition when he
1 Mr. Crothers.l
refused to settle this dispute twenty miles from Ottawa resulting in three deaths. I do not pretend to have followed the track of the leader of the Opposition when he was Prime Minister in refusing to intervene in Nova Scotia and when he said: ' Let them fight it out,' when he sent, through his Minister of Labour, his deputy to Nova Scotia, and gave him such strict instructions not to intervene lest he might lose a vote either from the workers or the owners, such strict instructions not to take any part as between the two sides to the dispute, that he was not able, he said himself, to ask them to meet a committee of one who did not belong to the United Mine Workers at all.
There is one other thing that I ought to mention. The hon. member for South Cape Breton' mentioned this matter, 'and, knowing the facts, 1 thought he ought to have been ashamed of himself to make any reference to it whatever. He sp ike abcut me not attending a meeting that had been called at Glace Bay. That is perfectly true, but what was the reason? We got stuck on the road and lost nearly half a day. I received a telegram from Ottawa telling me that the longshoremen at St. John, N.B., were threatening to strike and asking me to go to St. John as quickly as possible to try and avert the strike. Owing to the loss of time, owing to the fact that I was stuck in the mud, and owing to the further fact that I was obliged to return to St. John, a more important matter, I was not able to carry out the programme I had provided. Therefore, I went to St. John. There has been no strike. I do not say that my going to St. John was the reason of it, but it was my duty to go there in preference to going to Glace Bay. It1 was a very serious matter; there were eight or ten ships in the harbour of St. John waiting to load and the information came that they were threatening a strike. I did not go to Glace Bay simply because I was not able to carry out the programme for the reason which I have given. In the ordinary course I would have gone there in the interest of the whole country and not in the interest of any particular part of the country.

Mr. Speaker, I am compelled to make a few remarks at this late hour, but before proceeding I would like to ask you to request my hon. friend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers) at once to place upon the table of the House the letters from which he read

in the course of his address in reference to myself.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The rule is that when a minister of the Crown quotes from any official documents he is obliged to lay them on the table of the House.
Very well, Mr. Speaker, I shall do so right away.
The minister might as well do it at once.
Yes.

I am sure that the House and the friends of the hon. minister who has just sat down must have been somewhat surprised at the dignified, clear, and argumentative manner in which he made his defence to-night. It was worthy of a minister of the Crown in every respect,-[DOT]
Hear, hear.

And I am quite sure that the men who sit behind him, while they are applauding, are not very proud of the minister, when they consider the ridiculous position which he took in defending the actions of his department. Although on the stump and in the back woods, my hen. friend promised holus bolus to look after everybody who lost money in the Farmers' Bank, and things of that kind, once he gets into Parliament, while he fails to fulfil his pledges, he does not add by his methods any dignity to his position or in his dealings with public affairs. What does my hon. friend put forward as a reason why he neglected to attend to the ordinary business of his department in connection with this strike on Vancouver island? He says that there was a Buckingham strike in 1906, that- we did nothing, and that, therefore, he says: I did nothing. Splendid logic, is it not? Great statesmanship worthy of the Administration to which he belongs! That is the kind of argument in which he indulges, but the hon. gentleman, who did not follow the facts in regard to the matter, forgot there was not at that time on the statute book of this country the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, by which the Minister of Labour could deal with ,a question such as this.
There was the Conciliation Act.
You are misstating the facts now.

If the hon. gentleman has the pluck, let him stand up now and say that he did not take any steps with regard to this labour situation in Vancouver, because he was opposed to the United Mine Workers. I challenge him now to say whether that is his position, and I shall take my seat while he answers.
Speak.

The hon. gentleman will not answer, but that is really the position he has taken to-night. He has abused everybody connected with international labour unions. He has denounced the United Mine Workers and declared there was nothing in the allegation made by the committee with regard to gas in the mine. He has read decisions from judges elsewhere, which declared that the United Mine Workers should not be recognized, and then when he comes to the crucial point he has not the pluck to stand up and say that that was the reason he did not interfere in Vancouver. And yet, that is his whole defence to-night. He told us there was no gas in the mine-
There is plenty over there.

Not half so much as there is on the other side of the House. Let me read this statement from a man who was right on the ground and who will, I think, be accepted as being cognizant of the facts. The Rev. John Hedley, M.A., B.D., in an address before the Brotherhood of Haliburton Street Methodist church, said:
The Government have their inspector of mines, the companies have their fire-hosses, the men have their gas committee, elected by them and paid	These two_ men,_in June,
reported gas in dangerous cpiantity. This report was corroborated by the mining inspector. (See inspector's report.) One of these men shortly afterwards was dismissed by the company, and on going to Cumberland got work only to find later he was blacklisted. In the opinion of the miners he was discriminated against because of this report. The union protested through -a committee but the manager refused to see them. On the following day, September 16, the men took a holiday partially in protest, chiefly to collectively consider the matter. As the men were working on their different shifts of eight hours each this was only possible by taking a holiday. During the day a committee went to see the general. He replied 'that he did not know any of them and would not meet them.'
There, from the statement of a gentleman occupying a position in one of the Protestant churches of this country, we have the story of tne inception of this difficulty, from which it appears that it was sought to punish the men whose business it was to report gas in the mine, because they had so reported, and it appears from all the evidence that gas did exist there in dangerous quantities for some time before. This naturally interfered with the management to a very great degree. It threw upon them very great additional respons bility, which they did not care to assume. The summary method of disposing of the question was to dismiss the man who had found the gas. This they proceeded to do and to prevent him from being employed elsewhere. When the men resented this matter, they were told by the management that they did not know any of them and would not meet them. Yet my hon. friend, with those jaunting tours of his to the West in private cars and those tours of his across the ocean, while all these difficulties were occurring in the iYest, tells us that th s gentleman who gave this lecture right at the seat of the trouble did not know what he was talking about, when he declared and proved that the gas was the cause of the difficulty.
What else did my hon. friend say? tie said: ' Have I done anything I should not have done?' The great trouble with my hon. friend has been that he has not done anything at all. We are not finding fault with him for what he has done. He has left undone the things he ought to have done. His night and morning prayer with regard to this question should be that he may be forgiven for leaving undone the things he ought to have done. ' What have I done that I should not have done? ' he says. ' Nothing', we answer. Nobody during the last year has expected him to do anything -in his position. I saw_ in a British Columbia paper this reference to my hon. friend. Only to-day they are saying this in Tory, B.C.:
If the federal Government is wise in its day and generation, Minister of Labour Crothers will be retired to his village home.
We are not finding fault with the Minister of Labour for the things he has done. It is because of his desire to be called the Minister of Play instead of Labour, of h,s desire to jaunt across the country and across the ocean while serious d.fficuLies exist among the labouring classes in this country, that we are finding fault with the hon. minister, and certainly not for what he has done.	_
My hon. friend, in that illogical method in which he deals with his position, with that declination on his part to take any position, proceeds to tell us about this frightful, gentleman, Mr. Farrington, who had designs upon the coal mines of British Columbia. When he found that out, why he took to the woods. He did not go out and fight Mr. Farrington at all. He did not take any steps to bring this flight to a conclusion by intervening as he might have done, by asking for a conference of the men and of the management when he was out there himself, as he ought to have done, or by sending his deputy minister out there to deal with the question in that way. My hon. friend, if he knew Mr. Farrington was this menace, as he wants -this House to believe, should not have soughf quiesence; he should have been most active and aggressive in the interests of the people of Canada and the people of British Columbia, but he did nothing until to-night when he abuses. Mr. Farrington at long range as an excuse for not taking any action. He complains: How could I have known that they would go out on strike in May? Why does the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition say that I should have known that they would go
132*2

out on strike in May? Any real live Minister of Labour would have known, as a matter of course. If he knew that labour troubles existed on Vancouver island, as he was bound to know, and if he had means of information that any responsible minister would have at his command, he was bound to know that the condition was such that this trouble would naturally occur, and that a wider strike would take place in May. My hon. friend, who is paid to ascertain and know, complains when we say to him that he ought to have known.
My hon. friend tells us that the judges appointed by Liberals had given decisions in the West, sentencing these men who had taken part in riots. That is just about the size of the hon. Minister of Labour in his estimation of the men who held judicial positions in this country. With all deference to the gentlemen who sit around my hon. friend, I do not think there is one of his colleagues who believes that a man, who has passed through the strife and storm of political life, whether here or in any other political arena, who ascends to a judicial position, carries into that position any desire either to favour or to antagonize the people with whom he has been associated in his political days. Yet my hon. friend the Minister of Labour tells us that the judges appointed by the Liberals were the men who sentenced the strikers in British Columbia, and that argument shows the size of the man.
Then he tells us that my hon. friend from South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) was entirely wrong in regard to his statement about Orientals. Let us see about that. Mr. Price tells us something about Ori-enta's, and I think that my hon. friend from South Cape Breton is as accurate upon this question as I have always found him to be. This is what Mr. Price says in justification of my hon. friend:
It is true, however, that the number of Orientals employed underground in the mines of the Canadian collieries has increased very materially since last September, not only relatively, but absolutely, the total number of Orientals employed in May. 1913, being 432 out of a total [DOT]of 690, as against 315 out of a total of 766 in 1912, and probably among surface men the increase has been proportionately greater.
Then what does 'this clergyman say in regard to this question of disposition of Canadian labour in these mines, as the result of the action, or rather the failure to act, of the hon. Minister of Labour:
Later the Orientals who had stood loyaUy by their fellow-workmen, stated and generally believed, were intimidated to return to work. 
Since then the mines of Cumberland have been employing Chinese, Japanese, negroes and a few white miners.
So my hon. friend from South Cape Breton stated what was accurate. I am sorry that my hon. friend the Minister of Labour is not waiting to hear me out. This gentleman who I am told in Ontario is known as ' last speech Crothers,' does not seem to-night to like to have the second last speech. As he is a gentleman, who has explained to the world that he is not a Minister of Labour but a minister of play, and whose sole defence *to-night, when he was charged with maladministration is: What in the world have I done, when I have not done anything? I suppose he might as well be outside as inside when 'his department is being criticised.
What is the real issue in regard to the matter in the West? My hon. friend says that the strike in Vancouver island is ended. Here we have some statements to the contrary. The Western Call-my hon. friends from British Columbia will recognize it it is the last paper we have from them has this t-o say on the coal situation:
ine coal strike situation in British Columbia is quite unbearable. This is becoming, more and more, the opinion of right thinking men all over the province.	Especially do the
Inends of the Administration feel that some solution must be reached and that the situation ought to be at once firmly taken in hand by the Minister of Mines. The attitude of the Western Call has been sympathetic to the men and whilst deploring violence, which necessitated military and legal action, has persistently pointed out that no serious attempt has yet been made to bring matters to a head.
In fact, just what, we are saying here to-night in this resolution. (Reading):
In fact the public justly complain that they have been kept in the dark as to the real causes of the rupture between operators and men, and are growing steadily more impatient as they read of men for years-good steady citizens-being sent to the penitentiary for two years. Men who in no real sense can be called criminals. Men who have families to sustain, and whose past characters have been good.
But there is another reason why British Columbians are growing restive. The strike i3 seriously disturbing trade at a time when the province can ill afford it. Sixteen months of enforced idleness in one of the main industries of our province has helped to cause a stagnation in business that almost everybody feels, and the worst of it is that <iay by day our coal trade, one of our greatest sources of revenue, is being lastingly enfeebled by our coal users, unable to get coal at any reasonable figure, transmuting their furnaces into oil burners.
Coal is now being brought into the province from Australia-
.MARCH 3, 1914
That would worry my hon. friend from St. Antoine, Montreal; he never wanted to buy anything out in Australia.
-and advertised at $8.50 per ton. Household coal is $8 per ton, and we are only 30 miles from pithead, with a water haul from the bunkers. Coal can be put into the bunkers for $1.25 per ton at present wages. In Indiana and Illinois 10 cents a ton is reckoned a fair net profit for operators. This makes $1.35 per ton at bunkers. Between that and $8 or $8.50 there is surely a huge sufficiency to supply our coal scuttle without adding with it the sorrow and disgrace of a nearly two years' lockout of three or four thousand of our sturdiest workers. As a matter of fact $ 1 should give the operators a very splendid profit.
Something must be done. The public are demanding it now, and their voice will grow louder as the days go by.
That is from a paper which is a Conservative paper in British Columbia at this moment. And the Minister of Labour says that the strike is settled in Vancouver island. Certainly, a curious position of afiairs! Whait have I done? says the minister; I have done nothing. But what has he left undone? Why, he has not even pretended to do anything. What should he have done? His first duty was to find out the facts and place the responsibility for this trouble where it belongs. Did the hon. minister attempt to do that? Nobody wno reads Mr. Price's report will say that this was done. Mr. Price does not.even pretend to make findings on the question. After a long dissertation he winds up with the recommendation that there should be certain amendments to the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, and that is ail. What is the attitude of the men about investigation? In the British Columbia Legislature last week, Mr. Place, a labour representative, insisted, and public opinion fully concurred with him, says a newspaper, that it was the plain duty of the Minister of Mines to investigate the circumstances which led up to the trouble and to place the responsibility where it belonged. That is exactly what the miners asked and exactly what this Government was afraid to do. That is what the labour representative in British Columbia says,-that the duty of this minister was to investigate the question so that there- should be no doubt as to what were the primary causes of this labour difficulty and as to who was responsible. But the minister never attempted to do anything of the kind. When the business oi British Columbia is being paralyzed, and when for a year and a half destitution and proverty have reigned in what was a prosperous mining district, the minister has not yet
even tried to do that what was his first duty under the circumstances. The men say tin t that is all they want of the Government, and they are prepared to make their case. But the minister says:	Oh, I
did nothing because you did nothing at Buckingham and in Cape Breton. He was queried last winter, I think by myself, as to whether he was going to introduce amendments to the Industrial Disputes Act, and answered that he was not going to do so. If the statutory powers were not wide enough to enable him to deal with this question in such a way that the parties would be bound to come together after the facts were properly investigated and the responsibility for this strike had been placed upon the proper shoulders by a competent tribunal, why did not he come last session and take more extended powers? The hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) told us two weeks ago that the Minister was going to introduce amendments to the Act, but up to date he has not introduced anything, and we have no information as to what he intends. If the situation and the men in British Columbia are a menace to Canada, as the minister would have us believe, why has he not taken power so that he might avert from Canada the danger that threatens? It is this inertia that the Opposition in this House criticises, this inability to do anything, this carelessness as to whether anything is done or not so long as he remains Minister of Labour.
The hon. member for Nanaimo, after saying that he did not see that anything could be done,, he made a plea for the second time to the Minister of Justice to exercise clemency to the miners confined in the penitentiary, as I understand, for offences committed at the time of the difficulty. Whatever these men may have done, undoubtedly their offences against the law were committed in a moment of excitement and passion. I do think the hon. member for Nanaimo has strong ground of complaint against this Government at the retention in prison of these miners who, in a moment of irritation and excitement, may have committed offences against the law, in view of the fact that the Minister of Justice opened the doors to Landry, the forger, in Nova Scotia, and in view of the fact that Currie, the perjurer, after he had exhausted every means known to the law to escape from his confinement by judicial action, within a month the Minister of Justice opened the door and told him to be gone. Of all the offences

that are rank and smell to heaven, perjury has always been regarded as one of the worst. But these poor boys, who may have been misguided, and who, in the heat of the moment and in the feeling that is always roused on mining disputes, committed offences against the law, are told: You are not Conservative politicians, you must remain in jail while your children starve or anything else may happen.
Will the hon. gentleman make clear how long he says Currie spent in jail?

According to an
answer to a question in this House, which, strangely enough, does not appear in 'Hansard,' and which I have re-asked, he was sent to jail in the winter of 1913. His reserved case was argued in Halifax last summer, and before the Supreme Court of Canada in December. After the decision was given against him, he was liberated in the month of January.
Does the hon. gentleman know how long Currie spent in jail?
He was sent to jail in the winter of 1913.
So he spent a year in jail, which was longer than-

And his sentence was longer too. But the hon. solicitor general must not lose sight of the fact that Currie went to the Supreme Court of Nova Sc.tia on a case reserved and could not get out. Then he came to the Supreme Court of Canada on a special case in December and could not get out; and when the courts would not let him out, the minister did let him out. I sympathize with my hon. friend from Nanaimo in the complaints he makes regarding this matter. The Minister of Labour, certainly, in his policy of do nothing and know nothing, I suppose, never heard of this case in Nova Scotia, this discrimination as against the poor miner boys of the West; or if he had, he might posssibly have done something. Then, we should have said that he had done those things which he ought to have done. But instead of that the indictment is, and that indictment he has failed to answer, that he has left undone those things that he ought to have done.
Where, then, do we stand? The hon. minister has exhibited a total lack of interest in the lack of legislation in connection with labour in the two years and r half fMr. Macdonald ]
since he assumed his present position. A Minister of Labour has a great task to fulfil in this or any other country. The hon. gentleman has referred to distinguished men who have filled a similar position in the mother country. But whatever ambition he has to be classed in the same category as the men who have been presidents of the Board of Trade in Great Britain in times gone by, if he keeps on at the present rate, he will be regarded as not even having any conception whatever of what the duties of his office are. When a great strike occurred among the railway employees of Great Britain not very long ago, not only the president of the board of trade, but the whole Government were at once seized of the question and went to work with a view to overcome the diflieulty. On the contrary, the moment a big strike occurs in Canada, my hon. friend, forsooth, goes over to England to see how they do things over there. That is the part he plays in dealing with these labour problems in this country. Where is the line of legislation he has offered to Parliament since he occupied a seat in this House? Surely, after two and a half years of administration of a department, with all the development that has occurred in regard to these questiorfs in English-speaking countries and others, my hon. friend ought to have been able to find something that he might offer in the way of improvement of relations between capital and labour in Canada. But to-day he sits doing absolutely nothing so far as results are concerned, and his one defence is: thank God, he did nothing whatever for which he should be condemned. My hon. friend is supposed to have to do with the question of this Government and this Parliament taking a forward step in regard to technical education. My hon. friend has given no sign whatever that he has any views on that question. It is primarily a question that has to do with his department. So far as the Conservative press are concerned, so far as the indications one can gather outside go, my hon. friend does not propose, as a federal minister, to take any forward step in regard to technical education in Canada and, of course, if my hon. friend takes that position he will again be able to plead the defence that he did not do anything at all and therefore is not to be condemned. I have referred to the fact that my hon. friend has not attempted to deal in anyway whatever with the Industrial Disputes Act. But my hon. friend should remember

that a minister of the Crown has a right to so guide his department as to be able to defend himself from reasonable criticism such as hon. gentlemen were presenting to-night, without manifesting such a feeling of temper as he displayed. Imagine my hon. friend attacking as he has done the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville) ! My hon. friend's solicitude for labour and the rights of labour, has not been displayed in so great a degree of brilliancy either before or since he became Minister of Labour that it lies in his mouth to complain, of this worker representative who has been sent here as the representative of organized labour in this Parliament and as their spokesman? My hon. friend has no right to make the remarks he has of my hon. friend and colleague from Maisonneuve. The minister has not the confidence of organized labour, and as he knows that he naturally complains and becomes vituperative as regards the hon. gentleman who happens to have that confidence. I shall not labour the question. I submit that the evidence submitted to this House this afternoon proves conclusively the truth of the assertion contained in the resolution which we ask this House to adopt, that the story of my hon. friend's career as Minister of Labour is one of a do-nothing policy, that he has allowed a paralysing situation to develop in the West, without attempting to grapple with it, and that, in consequence, he is to-day receiving condemnation from the Conservative press of British Columbia, and he has a right to receive from this House that condemnation which this resolution would mete out to him if adopted in the terms in which it is moved.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this hour I shall not detain the House at any very great length, nor shall I say anything except with regard to the terms of the
1 a.m. motion which has been proposed by the hon. member from Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville). My hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) will forgive me if I do not go over the somewhat rambling speech wnich he has made.
I had to follow your minister, so we will leave it at rambling.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am glad my hon. friend will admit that it was a rambling speech; and I might say in passing that as he has alluded to the tone and manner of my colleague the Minister of Labour, I would
have expected a somewhat less agitated demeanour on his own part. However, under the circumstances, I am sure that a certain agitation of demeanour might well be forgiven to my hon. friend.
This motion is in somewhat peculiar terms:
Mr. Verville moves in amendment, seconded by Mr. Carroll, that Mr. Speaker do not now leave the Chair but that the whole conduct of the Minister of Labour in regard to the claims and rights of the coal miners of the island of Vancouver was marked by persistent negligence and absolutely indifference and deserves the censure of this House.
My hon. friend and colleague the Minister of Labour has alluded to a certain conference which went on yesterday in this House between the hon. member for Maisonneuve and the right hon. leader of the Opposition, and I would venture to say that while this motion was moved by the hon. member for Maisonneuve it bears the hall-mark of the right hon. leader of the Opposition. The hands are the hands of Esau but the voice is the voice of Jacob. Now, if we had a ' Hansard ' report of my right hon. friend's speech here to-night and could put it before him and could read it to him, I should say that for very shame's sake he dare not vote for that resolution on his own statement of the case. Mark the nature of it:
The whole conduct-
He does not attack any particular part, but the whole of the conduct of the Minister .of Labour-
The whole conduct of the Minister of Labour was marked by persistent negligence and absolute indifference and deserves the censure of this House.
And the right hon. gentleman who proposes to vote for that motion distinctly and positively stated that my hon. friend and colleague the Minister of Labour started out all right and kept on for a certain time all right. Now he proposes to eat his own words by voting for this resolution which says that the whole conduct of the minister is censurable.

He was all right for a
week.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Well, my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, not being able to speak for himself, has delegated that duty to the hon. member for Carleton.
I have not had an opportunity before tonight of reading over this correspondence

very carefully. Let us note one or two matters in connection with this. Already my right hon. friend has condemned the motion, because I took down his words as he uttered them. He held the Minister of Labour blameable in one respect only, namely, for not sending some person to investigate at an early date. That was the sum and substance of his challenge of the conduct of the Minister of Labour in this House; and notwithstanding that, he proposes in a few minutes to stand up and vote that the whole conduct of the minister was characterized by persistent negligence and absolute indifference. This is an illustration of the oft-repeated statement of my right hon. friend in this House that he is, after all, a partisan, because I think it would require not only a partisan, but the very strongest kind of a partisan to vote for that resolution after the exposition which has been given of the situation by my right hon. friend himself. The only challenge that he made from first to last of the conduct of the Minister of Labour was, that he did not send some person at an early date to investigate that matter; that is as far as I was able to understand his speech. If there was anything else in his speech, I challenge him to say what it was.
